utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Monday, the 8th of March, 2010. Let me first greet General Petkovic, all the accused who are present, the Defence counsel, and all the OTP members, the Prosecution, and everyone else assisting us. We will continue with the Prosecution's cross-examination. Today, the Prosecution should have another four hours and five minutes at its disposal, according to the calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We're just double-checking the time. We can check that, of course, with the Registrar and continue in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, each of you. Good afternoon, Counsel, all of those around the courtroom who are assisting us. And good afternoon, Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I want to spend a few minutes talking about the involvement of the Croatian Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, 1993, 1994 perhaps. When you testified in the Blaskic case, the representatives of the Tudjman government, as we discussed last week, Mr. Rifkin and Mr. Udiljak, would not let you answer questions about the relationship between the HV and the HVO. But continuing on from that topic, and the transcript that we looked at, which I'm sure you remember, what was the Tudjman government afraid of that it didn't want you -- wouldn't allow you -- wouldn't let you answer such questions in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object, because this is a question that calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe so, Your Honour. I believe the witness has knowledge, and it's obviously -- it's clear -- it's obviously been the Prosecution's case since last week -- well, long before last week, that this witness -- he may disagree, but it's our position that the witness was well prepared for the Blaskic testimony, that he had contact with a number of representatives, so we do believe that he was very well advised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when Mr. Rifkin and Mr. Udiljak would not allow you to answer questions in the Blaskic case about the relationship between the Croatian Army and the HVO, what was Tudjman afraid of -- Tudjman government afraid of that it wouldn't allow you to answer those questions?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know what the Tudjman government was afraid of. I don't know what sort of instructions Rifkin and Udiljak had. I don't know which questions they had in mind when they thought there were questions that they didn't want me to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But you agree that they intervened and prevented you from answering such questions, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They obtained such a position, and they intervened as other lawyers intervened here. I can't say why and with regard to which issues, but they fought to obtain this right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in the summary of your testimony -- your anticipated testimony that we were provided by your counsel, and as you know, that's the practice in the case, you indicated -- had you said that you arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the order, and I stress -- and I'm quoting from the second paragraph of your summary: " ... on the order of the HV commander of the southern army theatre, Janko Bobetko." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a decision from the Croatian Army. I agreed to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Janko Bobetko then appointed me to a position in the forward command post -- at the forward command post in Grude.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I didn't really ask you about -- a question about the decision of the Croatian government. What you say, what was given to us, and we were told that you would testify, is that you went to Bosnia-Herzegovina, quote, "on the order of Janko Bobetko." Is that true or not true? --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there one day earlier to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes or no. Did you go on the order of Janko Bobetko; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Janko Bobetko drafted an order. I didn't go there on his order. I agreed to go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my colleague is reading from a document that I drafted, could my colleague please read the sentence to the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The point, sir, is that sometimes you say you were ordered, and sometimes you say you went voluntarily. You went because you were ordered by Janko Bobetko, and that's what you've said in your summary, or is your summary -- or was the summary given to us not accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accepted to go, and then Janko Bobetko drafted an order when I arrived in Grude. The order wasn't drafted in Croatia; it was drafted in Grude, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you arrived again, just to touch on that, and we talked about this last week, when you arrived in Grude then, at that point you were still a senior officer in the Croatian Army, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had a decision according to which I was no longer a member of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How could Janko Bobetko give you an order to go to Croatia, an order that you were obliged to follow, if you were no longer a member of the army that he was the chief of?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the part when you say "in Croatia." Do you mean in Croatia or Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us that you arrived in the Grude -- around Grude on the 14th of April, 1992. You've told us, at least in part, that you arrived there on the order of Janko Bobetko, who was the head of the Croatian Army. My question to you: When you -- at the time you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina in mid-April 1992, you were still a senior officer in the Croatian Army, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, this being ordered by Bobetko, that's not exactly what you told the Judges in the Blaskic case, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said that Bobetko appointed me, he appointed Roso, and everyone else, too. I provided a list of all those who had been appointed by Bobetko. I provided all their names, at least as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You didn't, sir, you didn't. In the Blaskic case, you never mentioned Mr. Bobetko's involvement. On page 24210 of the Blaskic -- of your Blaskic testimony, 24210, the only thing you talked about, and I'll just quote part of it: "No one sent me to the HVO. I acceded to the HVO voluntarily." So -- and then skipping down, it says: "So no one sent me to the HVO, or, rather, no one wrote an order stating, Petkovic, you've got to go to the HVO." You didn't say anything about Mr. Bobetko's involvement when you testified in the Blaskic case, and again, sir, those were part of the instructions you received from Tudjman and the people around him, didn't you? When you go down there and testify, talk about being a volunteer, but don't say anything about Bobetko having ordered you to go. Those were your instructions, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I went there on a voluntary basis. Bobetko then drafted an order. You've seen that order -- or, rather, your colleague, as he could have shown the order and we could have discussed it, why that wasn't done, I don't know. Why did he show other orders, but not that one?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel, Your Honours, since the General has answered the question, let me just draw your attention to the following: My colleague, Mr. Scott, is trying to confront two different issues, to deal with two different issues. The first one is when Mr. Petkovic arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina and how. The second issue is how and when he joined the HVO. The general said that he arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that he was at the forward command post in the southern battle-field in Grude. And as for joining the HVO, well, that is a different issue, a different subject. So could we just be very precise so that no problems arise and there shouldn't be any requests for further clarifications in the course of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The reality is, sir, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please try and be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The reality is, sir, that despite whether someone should or should not have asked you a question -- the question differently, when you appeared in the Blaskic case in this same Tribunal, you said nothing about Mr. Bobetko or having received an order to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I read your Blaskic transcript two or three times, and Bobetko's involvement is not mentioned one time, sir; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Bobetko is mentioned in relation to some questions when they showed me certain documents, and I confirmed everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, it was only in the Kordic case a year or so later, and only when pressed by the Prosecution on that -- on your second court appearance at the Tribunal, that you then, in response to a Prosecution question, admitted to being -- some involvement by Mr. Bobetko; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first case, I answered all the questions put to me by the Prosecution. It's your problem if you didn't use the documents you had and if you didn't show them to me. I answered all questions put to me about each and every document, and I confirmed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you were playing a game. You were being very careful in answering questions very technically, but not volunteering truthful and accurate information to the Judges in that case; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what sort of a question is this, and on what basis is my colleague, Mr. Scott, putting this question to him? Is it the general's fault if the Prosecution in some other case didn't put certain questions to him? Could Mr. Scott say what constituted false testimony given by my client?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, so that we avoid wasting time, let's deal with this in the following way: Under oath, you said you went to Bosnia and Herzegovina, together with the Croatian Army, after the Serbian offensive had been launched. That's what you said. Why didn't you say that in the Blaskic case? Why didn't you say, I recognise the fact that the Croatian Army intervened in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to protect its borders, to protect Dubrovnik, because the Serbs might cut Serbian territory off if they had access to the sea, so we were there, and I went there following an order issued by General Bobetko? Why didn't you say that? It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was answering specific questions. Have a look -- or, rather, if you have a look at the beginning of my testimony at court, when the Presiding Judge said, We don't want to deal with that, General, let's deal with specific questions, well, in that introductory part I explained or tried to explain the entire situation. But the Chamber wasn't interested in that. They asked me to move on to a specific issue. So that entire part that I wanted to discuss, well, either there was a misunderstanding when preparing for my examination, but I skipped that entire part. I didn't even manage to say five sentences about that. The Trial Chamber asked me to focus on specific issues they were interested in. In that introductory part, I wanted to discuss the first day I arrived in the HVO, the organisation, the establishment of the HVO, and then I wanted to move on to specific issues. I think that this is in the transcript. You can see when the Judge asked me to deal with specific issues and not to deal with matters in a general way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you say if the question wasn't put to you, it's the Chamber's fault, or Mr. Kayway's [phoen] fault, who was incapable of putting the right questions to you. Very well. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in your curriculum vitae that we'd looked at last week, and I'm not necessarily going to stop again now - I'm sure I'll be corrected if I'm wrong - which is P08731, for the record, you said there, quote -- this is your CV: "On 14 April 1992, General Bobetko ordered me to go to the HVO." And that's true, isn't it? You were ordered to go by General Bobetko, the head of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not denying the fact that General Bobetko drafted an order. You have it. It's been shown five times in this case, the order to establish a forward command post that I was in charge of. Other HVO members were with me, and that is something that I do not deny. But I decided to join the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about the forward command post for a moment. Indeed, Bobetko established a forward command post of the Croatian Army in Grude and made you the commander of that Croatian Army forward command post when Mr. Bobetko wasn't there himself. And my next -- and you have no dispute about that, as I understand what you've just said. My question to you: When did the Croatian Army's forward command post, the one that you and Mr. Bobetko commanded, when did that command post become the HVO command or essentially, by whatever name, HVO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it immediately started performing certain tasks for the HVO, and in July most of its work concerned the HVO. That was July 1992. But there were quite a lot of orders regulating the status of the HVO, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, between -- so between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, just a minute. I have to be very fair to you. I looked at the questions that the Chamber wanted you to address, and, in fact, in the questions the role of the Croatian Army was not invoked. At no point was that invoked. It wasn't part of the questions you were to answer. At the very beginning of your testimony, the Presiding Judge referred to the questions that you were to deal with. I have just checked that. So, yes, in fact, this wasn't on the agenda. There was certainly a reason for that. It's just a hypothesis, but I believe that the Chamber must have "negotiated," in inverted commas, with regard to your hearing, and as a result, well, the Croatian government must have only agreed that you testify with regard to certain issues. And if the issue of the Croatian Army's intervention was part of the questions to be put to you, then they would have certainly refused for you to testify, and that is why the Judges weren't curious and they didn't put any questions to you, because it was part of the agreement -- of the contract. And proof of this is that President Jorda provides a list of all the questions. He was interested mainly in Ahmici, in the chain of command and the crimes committed in Ahmici. He didn't refer to anything else. So I believe that that is the answer. The Chamber must have seriously restricted the scope of the questions that could be put to you so that the Croatian government would accept you giving testimony. This is just a hypothesis I have, but if the issue of Croatian intervention had been on the agenda, then you giving testimony would not have been certain. This is why Mr. Kayway didn't come when the cross-examination was conducted. So that's perhaps the reason. Perhaps it was different in the Kordic case, but in Blaskic there were numerous difficulties, and that is why this wasn't on the agenda. Mr. Petkovic, what do you think about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, I really prepared myself to deal with my arrival in the HVO and the period right up until the 14th of April. That was how I had imagined my introduction. When the Chamber provided me with questions, that's what I understood the matter to be. When I started my testimony, the Chamber told me not to move in that direction. They wanted me to deal with certain specific issues. I wanted to give an introduction that would deal with my arrival in the HVO and the entire period through 1992 and 1993, but the Chamber quite simply said, No, we don't want to proceed in this way. And I think this is in the transcript, it says, then we have misunderstood each other. As to what the Croatian government discussed with them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 22442. This is what President Jorda says. He's very specific, very precise: "You saw, in your summons, that we want to put some questions that concerns certain information, that concerns the conditions in which you occupied this position, your appointment," that concerns General Blaskic's appointment, "we want information on the HVO organisation, on the system of communications, in particular on the chain of command. In brief, we want information on the situation that concerns all the units that Mr. Blaskic had under him and also that you had under yourself. You participated, either with General Morillon or Ambassador Thebault, in numerous meetings that had to do with implementing a cease-fire. We have also asked you -- or we will also ask you about your point of view on the discussions that you had with your enemies at the time. We would be very interested in any information you could provide us with regard to the crimes committed in Ahmici, which units were concerned, which units committed the crimes, were they HVO units, were they paramilitary units, were they under Colonel Blaskic's command or not? And, finally, more generally, how do you perceive the accused and his personality, who is one of your most direct collaborators during this very complex period?" These are the issues that were put before you. At no point in time was the issue of the Croatian Army raised. That is quite certain. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, be that as it may, the reality was whatever agreements that had been in place, at page 24210, 24210, Judge Rodriguez asked you specifically about how you had come to be in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as I read to you a few moments ago, your statement under oath was, and I'm reading directly from the page: "No one sent me to the HVO. I acceded to the HVO voluntarily." And at no point in answering Judge Rodrigues's questions about this topic, which he did ask about, did you mention Mr. Bobetko's involvement or any order from the Croatian Army, in terms of sending you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I think this has been asked and answered already. It has been, it has been, and it has been. Now, if you listen carefully to what the general has stated, he said he went there voluntarily. Obviously, he needed an order to go there. Now, the fact that one question wasn't asked of him by the Judge doesn't mean that he was lying. Now, the Judges can take his testimony as it is, but I think we should move on. We're wasting enough time. The Prosecution has argued that it needs more time to do cross-examination, but this is an abusive time and an abuse of the process. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no interpretation. I asked you to answer the question put to you by the Prosecutor. If you don't remember it, he'll put it to you again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could he please repeat it? I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point's been made, and I do agree with Mr. Karnavas on that point. And I had moved on, the topic came up again, so I went back. And I've read the transcript to the Chamber, and, of course, the Chamber will decide for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we were talking about the forward command post in Grude and when, at some point, it converted, if you will, from being the forward command post of the Croatian Army to being the headquarters of the HVO. And eventually you said something about, well, by around July most of what it was doing had to do with the HVO. And really, sir, that's what happened, isn't it? What had been the forward command post of the Croatian Army essentially converted and became the headquarters of the HVO. One day, it was the Croatian Army, and the next day -- or by July, it was the HVO headquarters, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. However, 95 per cent of those there were HVO members. I was the only one who had come from the Croatian Army voluntarily. All the others were members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, during this same time-period, and I think we've talked before, Mr. Tole came from the HV, Mr. Siljeg came from the HV, a number of officers had come from the Croatian Army around this time, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What really happened here, sir, isn't it true, is that the HVO essentially became the Croatian Army's forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten or eleven men performed the function of a forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, for all practical purposes, it was the HVO became the forward army of the Croatian Army, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO co-operated with the Croatian Army, and it had a unified front stretching from the Republic of Croatia to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we've talked in the course of your testimony and in the course of this case about joint armies or a joint command, and I put it to you: The HVO was far more a joint army with the Croatian Army than it ever was with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina between 1992 and 1994, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you there, because the Croatian Army, in July, went entirely towards Dubrovnik and we remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina until the end of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Wherever you were physically located, sir, you were effectively a joint if not the same army, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not. We were the HVO, and they were the Croatian Army. They had their part of the front, and we had our part of the front, and we co-operated along this unified front-line between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put to you that if you -- if it's your position, based on everything we know, that the HVO and the Croatian Army were not the same army, according to your criteria, then for sure the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were certainly not the same army or a joint army, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law passed in Bosnia and Herzegovina treats the HVO and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a joint army, and the Croatian law does not treat the HVO and the HV as a joint army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're not going to argue about the law, sir, because the lawyers will argue about the law later. But I put to you that your legal analysis is simply and completely wrong. But let me put it to you this way on the facts: Let's talk about the facts. You and the BH Army, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were very busy trying to kill and destroy each other, and I don't think that was the case ever between the HVO and the Croatian Army, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not right. We were not endeavouring to kill each other. We collaborated extraordinarily well for a long period of time, for longer than with the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I put to you, sir, that you were co-operating with the Croatian Army continuously from 1991 to 1994 and thereafter, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a single front. They held their men on the borders, and we happened to be next to them. So these two lines were linked and was transformed into a common front-line between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in the Kordic case, under oath, at page 26686, that you didn't know how the payments -- your income or the funds or -- paid to you or HVO soldiers: "Your Honours, I don't know who made the payments or how." And once again, sir, that wasn't true when you answered that question under oath in Kordic, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could two pages of the transcript from the Kordic case which refer to payments be shown to this witness, and that we could ask him for his opinion then, because colleague Scott is continuing to misrepresent answers of the witness in previous proceedings? He doesn't allow the witness to see exactly what was said, and in this way he's not contributing to the quest for peace. Could the witness be shown his answer to questions from the Prosecutor about payment, that there was no repetition by Judge Rodrigues six or seven times for him to answer questions about payments? So if we could do that, then the witness will certainly tell us exactly what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. If I may, I think it is absolutely inappropriate to ask the witness about his testimony 10 years ago and to expect him to give an answer based exclusively on his memory, so could we show him exactly what was said for that portion also to be interpreted in the witness's language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A point on the transcript. On page 17, line 9, this corresponds to the translation as I've heard it, Ms. Alaburic is referred to as speaking of "contributing to the quest for peace." I wonder whether you actually said that and wanted to say that, because I would rather have expected you of speaking of truth than peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my intention was to speak for the quest for the truth. If I misspoke, I apologise. And thank you for noticing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. It happens to all of us. You don't have to apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I'm looking at the page 26896 [as interpreted] in the Kordic case. I don't have the exact reference to the questions regarding payments. 26886.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I may have misspoke or someone misheard. It is page 26866.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you should have a binder available to you that's called "HV in BiH." If that can be -- if the witness doesn't already have it, if that could be provided to the witness, please. I'll refer the courtroom, please, to binder -- excuse me, a binder titled "Table - HV in BiH." If you'll turn, please, in that to P00910, there's a table on the front of that binder -- there's a table that's been provided on the front of that binder. There's also the documents behind the table. For reference to -- to assist everyone, it is line or item number 14 on the table, and it's been tabbed in the binder as number 14. There should be a sticky, so to speak, on the document number 14. Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just ask something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: It is my fault, of course. Which binder should we find that on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It is a binder that is -- probably has red tabs on the top, and it says on the outside "Table - HV in BiH." Tab 14, on the top -- there should be red tabs on the top. You find number -- if everyone finds number 14, that will be the same as P00910.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a request for funding that was going to Mr. Susak on the 15th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, you do.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it now. I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll look, sir -- even though the document -- the last page of the Croatian version is what is actually in the untranslated document. Although this document was to requesting funding from the State of Croatia to Mr. Susak, was prepared for Mr. Stojic's signature; that, in fact, was your signature, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can go to item number 19 in the table, or I will give you the exhibit number, also again tab 19 -- I'm trying to assist because the exhibit numbers were not in numerical order for various reasons. But if you can look at the red tabs, will you find number 18 in the same binder -- excuse me, number 19. My apologies. And, sir, this is a document from Mr. Berislav Pusic, dated the 6th of May, 1993, going to the Croatian Army in Dubrovnik. The second sentence: "It is necessary to have there a person from the HV Dubrovnik so that it would be easier to recognise the bodies of your dead soldiers." There was going to be a body exchange, as sad as that might be. If there was going to be a body exchange in a -- soldiers killed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what this -- what Mr. Pusic is referring to is that someone from the HV needs to come, it would be easier for them to identify the bodies of HV soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You didn't read it correctly, Mr. Prosecutor. It's an exchange of Chetniks, that is, Serb -- Serbian Army and the Croatian Army from the southern part of Croatia. As far as I know, Serbs and Croats in the south, that is, the Republic of Croatia and Republika Srpska, could not agree on an exchange of their dead, and then through the Observer Mission they proposed a neutral ground, and that is Herceg-Bosna. And it says "in exchange with dead Chetniks," and not an exchange of killed Croatian soldiers in Bosnia-Herzegovina who were within the HVO, as you endeavoured to put it. So this is an exchange of Serb soldiers and Croat soldiers who were killed in the south of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For the record, sir, this is Exhibit P02214. Can you tell us how Mr. Pusic then, for the HVO, came to be involved in an exchange between the Croatian Army and the Serb or VRS Army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was all done by the Observer Mission of the European Community that was stationed in Dubrovnik at the time and the Observer Mission which was in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were negotiating this. Why Pusic is there, I really have no idea. But, in any event, it is an exchange between the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in the Kordic case that in 1993 or in 1994, there were no Croatian Army units or elements in Central Bosnia. That was at page 26825 to 27. And, again, that wasn't true, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember a single soldier of the Croatian Army fighting in 1993 and 1994, as you put it, in Central Bosnia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll see what some of the other documents seem to show. In fact, sir, there were a number -- there were a number of the elements of the HVO -- the Croatian Army, excuse me. There were a number of elements of the Croatian Army that were active in Bosnia and Herzegovina during 1993, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about Central Bosnia. Certain elements of the Croatian Army may have been in Herzegovina, but we're talking about Central Bosnia, as that is what you asked me about. That is the zone of responsibility of Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when General Bobetko established another forward command post at Gornji Vakuf, General Bobetko and the Croatian Army called that Central Bosnia. And there were Croatian Army elements there, weren't there, in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1993. That is how I understood your question, 1993 and 1994. In 1992, there were certain volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And there were Croatian volunteers in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were volunteers. In 1993, there were no elements of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: You are overlapping each other, and I would like to ask both you of really to slow down a bit. I would ask also, actually, our President and everybody to slow down, because sometimes it is impossible to follow the declarations and questions and the answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to refer you to -- I'm going to be working largely from the table, but I'll give you the numbers. If we go to line number 16, which, for the record, is exhibit -- involves Exhibit P01332, P01332, line 16 - again in the binders it should have been marked with a red "16" - this is a document from Mr. Susak, and Mr. Susak talks about -- or, excuse me. The document talks about the payment of wartime allowances owed to soldiers of the HV 101st Brigade ordered by Susak and Praljak to the Southern Front, deployed by Commander Janko Bobetko. And the date of that communication is the 27th of January, 1993; not 1992, 1993. And you knew, sir, and you know now that there were elements of the Croatian Army continuously in Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout 1993, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where all these people were. They could have been south of Bregava, in the direction of Cavtat, or in the direction of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to item number --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then they are entitled to this allowance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to item number 28, which is P04061, P04061, in line 28. From Tole to the president of Croatia and the defence minister of Croatia, that is, Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Susak: "TG-2 will be under the command of the Southern Front. We ask you to help us in the following: "To send the 1st Battalion, if possible, from the 5th Guards Brigade who want to come to this theatre with complete equipment and weapons. To resolve the key problem," which is what the document is about, and it says: "To resolve the key problem around Gornji Vakuf." And that's the truth, isn't it? Croatian Army elements were active in the area of Gornji Vakuf continuously in the second half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not getting translation. There's no translation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were volunteers, and as you heard from General Praljak in his testimony, these were people with volunteer status. They were referred to in a document during General Praljak's testimony. There were about 230 of them, if I remember that document correctly. And it was submitted by General Praljak, and he was in Gornji Vakuf at the time, so he knows best.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. We have two questions here. When colleague Scott uses the term "elements of the Croatian Army," and the general answers with the words "men from the Croatian Army." When General Scott [as interpreted] uses the term "elements," is he implying men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the size of the elements?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I don't want to be involved in the situation you told us about in Blaskic case, where you were playing word games about this. You know what "elements" means, it's a commonly-used military term, and you know full well what it means. And whether they volunteered or not, and we'll put that to the side for a moment, whether they volunteered or not, these people were coming to Bosnia and Herzegovina as a unit -- as an element of the Croatian Army. They were part of the -- in some instances, they were part of the 5th Guards; in some instances, they were part of the 7th Guards; they were part of the 101st Guards, and you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were volunteers who had been born in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who decided amongst themselves to come, and they figured in the numbers they came. As for this group, I point you to the document in which 230 such people are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to line 40 in the table, which is Exhibit P05804, P05804, item tab 40. Tying a couple of issues or topics together, this appears to be an approval by Mr. Jelic of the Croatian Army to take 45 prisoners to the Heliodrom. Do you see that? Mr. Jelic doesn't say that they were being taken by individuals or volunteers. He says they were being taken by the Croatian Army; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where that Croatian Army could have been at this point in time on the 11th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we draw attention to the full stop after the letter H and after the letter V, which could indicate that this could be the name of a unit. General, could you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hrvoje Vukcic could be the name of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I object to the procedure. It's not for counsel to get up and tell the witness what the answer should be, and I strongly object to that. It should not be allowed. And I take it that its withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you know what that means, and you know there were Croatian Army elements in that region at that time, but I don't want to spend -- I don't want to get us too bogged down in this, but -- because there's over 50 documents, there's 40 some documents in this. We don't have time to go through them, unfortunately. I wish we did. But look at line 41, Exhibit P07423, a report by Mr. Skender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, regardless of this, do you recognise that the document that comes under tab 40, Exhibit P5804, does not illustrate your theory on the presence of the Croatian Army, because in the text, after the H and V, there is a full stop. And the unity [as interpreted] was Hrvoje Vukcic, so it doesn't stand for the Croatian Army. So do you recognise that you made a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With great respect, Your Honour, no. I think it's up to interpretation. "HV" is HV, and that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But "HV" is written without a full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It might be in most instances, sir, but there's no point in us arguing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you would go, please, and follow my instructions, go to tab 41, P07423, Mr. Skender reports: "HV unit, 7th Guards Brigade, 1st Battalion, was engaged in fighting against MOS," Muslim armed forces or defence forces, "in the Uskoplje battle-field, Gornji Vakuf, in an attempt to protect Croatian Army in HR-HB. This unit was carrying out offensive and defensive tasks." The 7th Guard Brigade is an element of the Croatian Army, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 7th Guards Brigade, yes, but members who volunteer are something quite different from the 7th Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They're still the 7th Guards, sir, aren't they? They may or may not have volunteered, but when they go, they may say, just like you -- you said, General Bobetko, I'm willing to go, you can order me to go, I'm willing. But when you went to Croatia, you were still a member of the Croatian Army, weren't you? It didn't matter whether you volunteered, sir. You went under Bobetko's order, subject to your superior, as a member of the Croatian Army, and whether they volunteered or not, they were still members of the Croatian Army, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they were born there, and they had every right to leave the Croatian Army and go --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You say they were, sir. Did you see their birth certificates of each one who went?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, General Petkovic, the document that we have in front of us, and that could have been presented to Colonel Skender when he was there, it indicates that the elements of the Croatian Army were engaged against the BiH Army, and then the Colonel Skender sent that document, which is indicated in the left part of the document, to the Croatian Army. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when we read this document, we could perhaps start thinking that there was a military operation involving units of the Croatian Army on the 31st of December, 1993. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, one could interpret that, but it was about the 70 members of the Guards Brigade, and those were all people who hailed from the territory of Herzegovina or, rather, Bosnia and Herzegovina, who had decided to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina even at the cost of perhaps losing their status in the Croatian Army. At this moment, we still had 10.000 of our own men who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina and are still members of the Croatian Army, and we are still waiting for them to come back, and they're coming in batches, 50, 70, 100. Look at the officer here. He was in command of a small group, and that group had about 70 men from the 7th Guards Brigade. And I believe that Mr. Mandic was in -- its commander and he hailed from Siroki Brijeg. He was its first commander, and the second commander was Branko Preradovic, or I'm not sure about his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So what you're saying is that for you, those were volunteers because they were all born in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they hailed from those territories and they went there. And in the Croatian Army, you can see where the 7th Brigade and other brigades were engaged with the main body of their troops at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question was pending to you, sir, at the time, and I'll repeat it: You don't know that these people were all born in Bosnia and Herzegovina, do you? That might be the party line, but you've never seen all their birth certificates, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see their birth certificates, because nobody carries birth certificates into combat. But we knew where they hailed from, and we knew that they went home when they returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you say, sir, so you say. If we can go to tab 42 in the table, which is P07475. P07475, tab 42. This is part of a presidential transcript on the 4th of January, 1994. I'll direct your attention and the courtroom's attention to page 14 -- starting on page 13, perhaps. Mr. Bobetko and Mr. Susak, and perhaps others, but at least those two, are meeting with President Tudjman. At the bottom of page 13, Mr. Bobetko is giving a report. Carrying over to the top of page 14: "And it is all organised, but this shift, 7th Zagorska Guards Brigade, a part of it has not shift changed yet. It should be done these days. They are holding Gornji Vakuf, 200 of them, and they are very good at it. I said to Petkovic today, that now, today, a new mobilisation should commence, and I ordered that this 8th Light, holding positions at another location, Ogulin, as a reserve be transferred down there for manoeuvre or that we go up there towards this part in the direction of Travnik." And that's accurate, isn't it? Mr. Bobetko had talked to you on the 4th of January, 1994, about rotating the 7th Guards out of Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. General Bobetko didn't speak to me. He had requested me. And there is also information that the 7th Brigade and the Light Assault Brigade was never in Gornji Vakuf. You have the minutes of a meeting which took place on the 7th of January with a list of all the units that were there, and those units were not there. This is just a story, and I claim that these two never arrived at Vakuf. These two units were still in Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look at Exhibit P07884, which is -- excuse me, table -- tab 14 or item 43, P07884. This is a report, sir, from the 8th Light Assault Brigade in the Croatian Army. It's a Croatian Army document confirming, in fact, the rotation in mid-February 1994, and it begins by saying: "Pursuant to the verbal order of the chief of the Croatian Army Main Staff of 13 February 1994, and concerning the hand-over of the area of responsibility of the 8th Light Assault Brigade to HVO Defence units on the 15th of February, a commission was formed..." et cetera. And the document goes on to record the transfer.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is not Gornji Vakuf. This is from the border of the Republic of Croatia towards Buna, towards Buna. This is not Gornji Vakuf. I'm telling you that the Light Assault never arrived in Vakuf. Half of it was in Matkovic, and the other half was in the direction of Dubrava Plateau. And if you look at all the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where is Buna?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: South of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the HV -- so putting aside anything else for the moment, this confirms that an HV unit and the HVO were rotating responsibilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina just south of Mostar, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to the area south of Mostar, but not to Gornji Vakuf, as you said at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we now know where Buna is and where the rotation is taking place. Sir, isn't it correct that -- give me a moment, please. Mr. Davor Marijan, who testified in this case, also testified as a Defence expert in the Tuta Stela case, and in that case Mr. Marijan identified the 5th Guards Brigade -- the Croatian Army 5th Guards Brigade as the most involved HV unit in BiH in 1993. He said that the 7th Guards Brigade was the second-most involved HV unit. The 1st Guards Brigade, known as the Tigers or Tigrovi, were also actively involved. The 2nd Guards Brigade, known as Thunders or Gromovi, were actively involved, and he identified all those units as being in Bosnia and Herzegovina during 1993. Are you saying that's not true?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't accept what he said. Some elements were there, but not more than 50, 60, or 70 men from each of these brigades, and they were only people from Herzegovina, or, in other words, volunteers in the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you'll go to Exhibit P03667, which may be a loose exhibit, Your Honours, but it's P0 -- it's not in the table, it's not in the binder we've been looking at in the last few minutes, at least I don't think so, but it's P03667. Sir, this is a report from Mr. Kapular, commander of a Croatian Army unit, dated the 23rd of July, 1993, in which Mr. Kapular is reporting to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia concerning an action on the Southern Front involving the 5th Guards Brigade; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about volunteers from the 5th Brigade who participated in the Operation South in the month of July 1993 south of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the Chamber has seen this document before, but in that paragraph numbered 2 on the second page of the English version, but it's under heading 2, I'll remind you that Mr. Kapular says, essentially, nobody is fooled by calling it the Southern Front; everybody knows what the Southern Front really means. And that meant, in this instance, Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Southern Front was the Republic of Croatia and the area behind the borders towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that group was engaged in the Southern Front because that was south of Mostar, which was exactly in the area bordering on Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, by some definition, sir, we can all agree that's some distance from -- some kilometres from Mostar, there is the Croatian border. I think we can all agree on that. But these people were acting -- in the 5th Guards were acting inside the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying the area around the borders in Bosnia-Herzegovina and parts of the Republic of Croatia together were considered the Southern Front. This was a unified Southern Front.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, 1993, sir, you were still the head of the HVO Main Staff, and you knew at that time, didn't you, that by that time, by the middle of 1993, if not sooner, Herceg-Bosna and the HVO government and military leadership knew that without the support and involvement of the Croatian Army, it was going to be very difficult for the HVO to establish its objectives, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been difficult even for the Republic of Croatia, because the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina wanted to take part of the Republic of Croatia also, the sea -- the coastal area. Yes, it was very difficult to defend the southern part of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to -- I'd like some assistance, please, and I'd like you to listen specifically to my question and answer my question and not some other question. The leadership -- the governmental and military leadership of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO knew, by the middle of 1993, that it would be very difficult for them to establish their objectives without the active support and involvement of the Croatian Army, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objectives were to defend the area and not allow a breakthrough to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, sir. I didn't ask you what the objectives were. Please answer my question. Don't answer another question. Answer my question, Mr. Petkovic. The leadership knew --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think if we look at the question, and everybody should just calm down a little bit - I'll be the first one to admit I get a little excited at times - but I think if you look at the question, Your Honours, it's extremely difficult. It's almost like -- well, I won't use the example that is always used, you know, When did you stop beating your wife, sort of question, but it's as posed -- now, if we go step by step, I understand there's some time limitations, but I think the Prosecution is overreaching at this stage and is assuming facts that are not in evidence, is speculating. So step by step, and I'm sure, you know, the gentleman is quite capable. I'm rather impressed, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to put it in, perhaps, a bit simpler way. Reaching their objectives, is what you say, but which objectives? So far, we get the impression from the Bench -- I get the impression that you have one idea of what the objectives were, and the accused, the witness, has always denied this. So probably it's difficult to put this question in a way which does not lead back to the lower grassroot question of what were the objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Sorry if I've created confusion. My point is I don't want to argue with the witness now about what the objectives are. He said, at least for these purposes, that they were the defence of the territory of Herceg-Bosna. Now, whether I agree with that or not, for the purpose of this question, I accept that, for the purposes of this question. So my question remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The HVO, Herceg-Bosna leadership, the political, the governmental, and military leadership, knew that by mid-1993 they would have great difficulties if, in fact, it would not be impossible to achieve their objectives, however you define them at the moment, without the active support and involvement -- in fact, on-the-ground involvement of the Croatian Army; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What objectives? What are we talking about? Is it -- excuse me. Is it the objective to mount a proper defence against the Serbs? That's one. Is it to co-operate with the ABiH in certain areas where there is co-operation against the Serbs? Is it the situation in Central Bosnia? There is a host of things. Now, if the Prosecution could say, I put it to you that these were the objectives, he could say, Yes, or, No. And then even if he gets annoyed, he would say, Well I still put it you, an X, Y, and Z. I think that's the way it's normally done. And then he could follow up with whatever information he may have, once he has locked the witness into his position, to demonstrate so that we can all see, ha, ha, ha, now we know what he means by "objectives." But thus far, I think it's rather vague and it's improper. And I think some of my other colleagues would like to chime in, but I don't think that this is a proper way of cross-examining, at least on this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, when you speak about objectives, I believe - maybe I'm mistaken - that you're talking about the objectives of the joint criminal enterprise. Is that what you have in mind when you are putting this question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was trying to avoid all these issues by just accepting, for these purposes, what the witness, himself, said the objectives was. But apparently that doesn't seem to be working, so I'm going to go on to another question. I thought it was rather clear, but I'm not going to take the time to pursue it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This action that Mr. Dzanko was involved in that you've described as Operation Jug, you've told us during your direct examination that you said -- excuse me. On the 15th of July, 1993, you met with Mr. Boban in the evening, and that was when, according to you, you told Mr. Boban that you wanted him to find a replacement for you, that you would give him something like 10 days to find a replacement. You recall that testimony, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at the time, sir, you knew full well that Operation Jug, as it was ultimately planned and carried out, was an HV-led operation, wasn't it, a Croatian Army-led operation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not. There were volunteers and there were two HVO brigades under the command of Luka Dzanko. I don't know what his status was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you know full well that Mr. Dzanko was a senior Croatian Army officer and that the HV 5th Guards Brigade -- the 5th Guards Brigade that we've been talking about this afternoon was substantially involved in this operation, supplemented by some elements from the HVO. And, in fact, you wrote a report on this with Mr. Dzanko, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just correct you. You can't say some elements of the HVO. There were two HVO brigades which were four times bigger than the whole body of volunteers from the 5th Brigade. The 1st and the 3rd Brigades which were much bigger than the group of 350 volunteers from the 5th Brigade who arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit P03466, P03466. I believe it's in binder 1, I've been told, but we're still checking. Perhaps we can also -- if it's pulled up in e-court, we can work -- it's loose. I'm told now, and I apologise to the courtroom, that it's a loose exhibit, P03466. He's got it. Sir, this is a report that you and, I believe, Mr. Dzanko authored together, indeed, dated on the 15th of July, 1993, and you report this event, this action. You talk about "our forces" on the second -- at least in the second page of the English version, but you'll find it, "our forces," in the Croatian version. And you see that it talks about 400 men from the HV 5th Guards Brigade for the attack. And Mr. Dzanko is listed, I might indicate here, on this document, since you questioned it a moment ago, deputy commander of the Split Military District, Brigadier Luka Dzanko. And you knew full well -- sir, when you sat there on the 15th of July, 1993, and drafted this report with Mr. Dzanko, you knew full well he was a senior officer in the Croatian Army, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that he was an officer of the Croatian Army. And, second of all, do you know where this document was drafted? This document was not drafted at the HVO. The HVO did not have such a code. Luka Dzanko sent this document on his own from Ploce to General Bobetko, and that's the whole truth. The HVO is not represented by this code. You saw what the HVO used and how it used it. Look at the stamp. This is not the stamp --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're wasting time, sir, and you know it. This is a document that you and Mr. Dzanko prepared together about this action, and you're avoiding the question and the answer that's obvious, and that is: Mr. Dzanko was a Croatian Army commander in command of this unit which was substantially carried out by elements of the 5th Guards Brigade; yes or no? If you don't agree, sir, just say, No, and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct. Yes, he was the deputy commander of the Split Military District. He was the second in command in the Military District of Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, in fact, your knowledge of what happened in Operation Jug and the fact that this was -- and I put it to you that it was a Croatian Army operation, under Croatian Army command, that very event was one of those that President Tudjman and the people that met with him on the 13th of April, 1999, that we looked at last week, were concerned about, that you knew that this was an HV operation, and that if you went to testify in The Hague, that was something that might come out, wasn't it? Can we go to Sanction slide --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go to slide number 25, which is an excerpt from page 39 of Exhibit P08192. Mr. President, this is the same presidential transcript that we looked at last Thursday. Mr. Cosic, who we identified as the deputy defence minister of Croatia: "Mr. President, in August 1993, after the 5th Brigade suffered that defeat, and so on, we sat in the cellar, General Petkovic, General Djuric and Luka Dzanko, and a letter was written ..." And I put to you, sir, that 3466 is the letter that you prepared with Mr. Dzanko. And it goes on to say: "He came in about 1993. He was engaged there from the HVO. He used to be in the former JNA." And then they realised that they were talking about the wrong person, but then goes on to say: "So General Matic and General Petkovic, Mr. Boban was there, and General Petkovic knows too much, so I think the risk is too great for us to put him into an uncertain environment which is not friendly." Sir, the very thing that these men were concerned about your knowledge of was the Operation Jug and your knowledge that, in reality, it was a Croatian Army operation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, why would -- Jug be a Croatian Army -- why would Operation Jug be an operation of the Croatian Army? Nobody but Cosic mentions Operation Jug, and your colleague could have asked me anything he wanted, and I knew a lot more about other things as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You may have, and again I know you want to blame the people asking the questions, but Mr. Cosic, who is the deputy defence minister of Croatia, what Mr. Cosic says is "After the 5th Brigade suffered that defeat ..." And I assume that the assistant minister of defence of Croatia knows the elements and units of the Croatian Army, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he knew. Kapular sent a report to the Ministry of Defence. The unit commander sent a report to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in this case you've sat here under oath in this Prlic case, you've been sitting here for three and a half years, you know the involvement of the Croatian Army in Bosnia and Herzegovina is an issue in this case, you know that full well, and you sat in front of these Judges, under oath, and talked about Operation Jug, and you never once informed them that this, in reality, was a Croatian Army operation, commanded by a Croatian Army officer. You sit here -- sat here and misled these Judges and allowed them to believe something that wasn't true, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my intention. I did say that two HVO brigades participated in that and that their strength was much bigger than the HV movement, because there were some 4.000 members of the HVO that participated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, I would like to say that Mr. Scott misinterprets what has been happening in this courtroom, and I am saying this with full responsibility, because the Petkovic Defence has very clearly stated that the commander of the Operation Jug was Luka Dzanko. That was not in dispute, and it was also not in dispute that he was a Croatian Army officer. And it was also not in dispute that volunteers from the 5th Guards Brigade of the Croatian Army participated in that operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All that is in the transcript. Mr. Scott, it's perhaps time for our break now. Now, the Registrar has calculated the time you have used. You've used up 5 hours and 12 minutes, so you have another 3 hours and 40 minutes available.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have our 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I want to turn now to the topic of some dealings or relationship between the HVO and the VRS, the Bosnian Serb armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm putting now slide 51 -- Sanction slide 51 on the screen. You testified in the Blaskic case, at page 24123: "General --" The question was asked: "General, did you and the HVO participate with the Serbs against the Muslim -- or the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?" Petkovic answer: "No, we never acted together with them." And, sir, I'm going to ask you once again, as you've heard me ask you several times now: That testimony that you gave in the Blaskic case is not true or correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never took joint action with the Serbs. But as for weapons and equipment, to the extent that it was possible, we obtained such weapons and equipment from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, both of you. I believe that there was an important mistake in the question asked by Mr. Scott. The question was asked, and I quote: "General, did you and the HVO participate with the Serbs against the Muslims -- or the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?" I believe that the question was, if I'm not mistaken: "General, did you and the HV participate ..." Was it your intention to ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, it is "HVO."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, you say today that, in fact, you participated with them or dealt with them in some ways in terms of obtaining arms and all that, but once again, sir, you very clearly -- when you testified in the Blaskic case, you very clearly attempted to create the impression, before those Judges, that there was no co-operation or dealings -- no co-operation between the HVO and the VRS at all, didn't you? I agree you've changed your position, I'm putting that to you. But the impression you tried to create in the Blaskic case was, very categorically, there was no involvement, no dealings, no co-operation. That's what you wanted to tell those Judges, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The question had to do with Vlasic -- in co-operating with the Serbs on Vlasic. A document was shown. The Serbs allege that this was done for propaganda reasons, and that's what the testimony had to do with. As far as I can remember, I believe I said that we and the Muslims obtained weapons -- or, rather, ammunition from them. The specific question put to me concerned Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it was only again, sir, in the Kordic case when, again, once you were pressed and when documents were put in front of you, that you then agreed for the first time that there was trading and dealing between the HVO and the VRS, in terms of acquiring weapons and ammunition, starting with at least the beginning of July 1993; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given that last Thursday my colleague Scott falsely alleged that the Judge Robinson put a question on six or seven occasions, I would appreciate it if he could lay a factual basis for the question just put.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Your Honour, I disagree that I gave any false information about Judge Robinson's repeated questions to the witness before he finally got an answer. Whether I said seven or eight, there were numerous questions, and I'm happy to let the Chamber review the transcript and count them for themselves. But I'm absolutely confident it was only after repeated questions by Judge Robinson that the question was finally answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, how often were you -- was the HVO and Serbs involved in these dealings, and how often were you involved in approving these transactions between the Serbs and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until -- or while the ABiH had us surrounded and wanted to defeat us, during that period of time the only way of obtaining ammunition was to try and buy it from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how often were you directly involved in those negotiations or directing other HVO agents who were involved?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say how often, but I issued instructions saying that such equipment could be obtained because that was the only way that the Croats could survive in Central Bosnia and defend themselves from the ABiH army. It was also impossible to get from Herzegovina to Central Bosnia. Not a single route was open for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you dealt, sir, with -- you were -- in fact, sir, you were the principal negotiator, ultimately, on behalf of the HVO, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you were actually dealing directly at times with Mr. Mladic from the Serb army or the VRS, weren't you, Ratko Mladic, this Tribunal is well familiar with? You and Mr. Mladic frequently dealt with each other to arrange these transactions, didn't you? And I'm going to tell you, sir, if it will help you -- I'm going to show you a number of documents that will indicate exactly that. So if you want to deny your involvement with Mr. Mladic, I suppose you can do so.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever the UNPROFOR commander called me when I arrived in --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're not going to waste time talking about that. My apologies to the interpreters. I do apologise to the interpreters, but time is precious. I asked you nothing about UNPROFOR, sir. You frequently dealt directly with Ratko Mladic, didn't you; yes, no?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that I had frequent contact with him. I attended meetings, if necessary. I had time to reach agreements at those meetings that were organised by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you know full well that you had numerous dealings with Mr. Mladic, and it had nothing to do with UNPROFOR; that you were communicating with him to arrange transactions between the HVO and the VRS. And you know that, sir, and you're being dishonest with this Chamber to represent otherwise, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Others had contact with him, but I had enough time, for example, at meetings at the Sarajevo Airport, to say, I need such and such equipment. If possible, could it please be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it your position, sir -- is it your testimony, under oath, that the co-operation between the HVO and the VRS was limited only to arms trading?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, to arms trading and to the possibility of using the road to Vares -- or, rather, towards Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, isn't it the case that most of what we've heard in this trial about any real armed conflict between the HVO and the Serbs in the area of Herzegovina, between late 1992 and at least until March 1994, that was all really phony, wasn't it? And I use the word "phony" specifically. It was false, it wasn't real. It was all kind of a put-on -- a put-up job, so to speak, that you would like this Chamber to believe you were engaged actively in a war with the Serbs during that period, but you weren't, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were actively engaged in a war against the Serbs, and that was more the case than for our associates up until then, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I put it to you, sir, that between December of 1992 and March of 1994 in the area of Herzegovina, there was not a single significant armed conflict between the Serbs -- between the VRS and the HVO; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. Our lines were actively engaged. We had dead men, wounded men. The artillery and tanks and the infantry were active.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You say that, sir, but you're not telling us anything. I'm not talking about the fact that there were two lines looking across each other across some distance. I'm talking about active military operations, offensive operations. Please identify for me a VRS offensive operation carried out in Herzegovina against the HVO during 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1993 there were several operations in the direction of Nevesinje. There were several operations from Bugojno to Kupres, in the direction of Kupres. And there were some operations in the area of Vlasic, in the Travnik area, and incessantly in the valley of the River of Usora and Komusina village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Give me the dates of those events and how long they lasted, and the size of the units that were involved, because I put to you, sure, there may have been some local skirmishes here and a skirmish there, an artillery shell here and there, but there were no sustained major HVO-VRS actions during 1993 in Herzegovina, were there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which actions you're referring to. Do you want operations that involve depth of 100 or 200 kilometres? We were waiting for allies -- our allies to invite us to join in operations against the Serbs, large-scale operations against them. We did what we could. That concerned tactical depth, moving the lines, defensive lines --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, you're avoiding my question, and you know it. And, again, don't blame -- you always blame it on somebody else; it's the Court's fault, it's the questioner's fault, it's the Muslim's fault, it's Izetbegovic's fault. It's always somebody else's fault, sir. You didn't answer my question. Tell these Judges right here, under oath, one significant large-scale offensive operation between the HVO and the VRS in the region of Herzegovina in 1993. Tell them.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were large-scale operations in the area of Tomislavgrad-Livno at the beginning of 1993, in Bugojno, Kupres. There were operations in the Valley of Usora and in the Valley of Kamusina, where we managed to drive back the Serbian forces in a significant way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to the testimony of Mr. -- again, the Defence expert Davor Marijan, who testified in this case and in the Naletilic case. Slide -- Sanction slide 52, at page 15601-03. My question to Mr. Marijan in that case: "Sir, any violence, of course, is too much, and there were certainly skirmishes and artillery shells fired from time to time, but isn't it true, sir, that in 1993 in the Prozor-Mostar-Stolac region, fighting between Serbs and Croats was not a significant factor in what was happening there?" Answer, under oath: "That is true." And you know that to be true, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look. If a soldier who spent a short period in the HVO -- well, if he knows more than the Chief of Staff of the HVO, well, then he really is an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, he was called as an expert, sir, twice, not by me. He was called by two different Defence teams as an expert, so apparently someone thought he had some expertise.
