Sir, if you could go to slide -- if we could have Sanction slide number 53, let's look at what was being said on this topic by President Tudjman during this -- in President Tudjman's office during this period. I'll put these to you, and then I'll ask you a couple of questions. The 2nd of September, 1993, Exhibit P04740, pages 9 and 10: "Tudjman: ... we can't allow accusations of direct military involvement of Croatia in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and on the other hand, all state organs in all areas naturally have to provide help to that Croatian republic, not only to survive but to prosper and be a support for the Croatian state. "In view of this situation, we have to suppress relations with Belgrade ... it is a fact," and he's making this statement on the 2nd of September, 1993, "it is a fact, though, that for five or six months now there has been no fighting between the Croats and Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina." On the 15th of September, 1993, Exhibit P05080, pages 18 to 20, Mr. Praljak is speaking: "Another thing is, the relations between the Croats and the Serbs have improved, especially on the military plane, because our whole units depend on co-operation with the Serbs ... therefore, Zepce, Kiseljak and thus Vitez, the battalion below Konjic and Vares, it will now be difficult for us to provide them with supplies. "Tudjman: But the fighting against the Muslims should stop. "Praljak: It will stop, but this is going to be different --" or "difficult," I think, and I would submit -- and we can look at the transcript, but I believe that should be "difficult": "A year ago, we thought we could not hold talks with the Serbs at all. We reached some agreement with the Serbs, and now we should start a war against them in order to ease the tension with the Muslims, and it will probably take time to turn things around, psychologically. "Susak: Their side, we should say something to the media. We cannot simply neglect the Serbs now. The point of this agreement is a cease-fire. It is not unification and war against the Serbs. We must inform the public in a subtle manner that we are not establishing a union with the Muslims to fight the Serbs ..." The 12th of January, 1994, P07570, pages 55 and 56: "Tudjman: Jadranko, take steps to open Croatian offices in Banja Luka: "Pranjic: We discussed this and they agree, but someone has to carry this out. We must be sufficiently prompt and flexible as regards this matter ... "Tudjman: We must act in both directions, both towards the Muslims and the Serbs, to get out of this infernal situation. "Jadranko Prlic: Everything can be agreed upon with the Serbs, Mr. President - joint military activity and a military alliance and everything else. There is no operational matter ..." Now, I'm going to stop there for a moment, sir. You know, based on what Mr. Davor Marijan has testified at this Tribunal under oath, by the comments by the Croatian government leadership, that that's the state of -- that was the state of affairs, wasn't it, in 1993, or at least much of it -- most of it? There was no fighting between the VRS and the HVO, and any allegations to the contrary are deceiving this Chamber, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. In June, the Croats were totally cut off in Central Bosnia by the Muslims, and they couldn't establish contact with the Serbs and fight with them. That's what the period is about here. So as of June, the Muslim aggression against the HVO blocked the entire HVO system. They had surrounded them, broken it up into small areas in Central Bosnia, and the concern was quite simply to defend oneself. In such conditions, you cannot attack the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, exactly, sir, exactly. You weren't fighting the Serbs during this time-period at all. Let's go -- in fact, sir, you know -- you know, and the Croatian leadership knew, that in reality the war between the Croats and the Muslims was much worse than the war between the Croats and the Serbs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Muslim aggression was more intense than the Serbian one. They had surrounded us wherever that was possible for them, and we had no contact -- our enclaves didn't have any contact between themselves. And under such conditions, you can only fight those surrounding you. Those surrounding us were the Muslims or the ABiH. I think that we have demonstrated what was going on in June. The HVO was completely isolated and had no way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thirteen of February, 1994 -- I'm sorry. If I wait for translation, Mr. Petkovic just continues on, and I don't have time to allow that. I apologise. 13th of February, 1994, P07856, Mile Akmadzic, a witness in this case: "I would only remind you that yesterday Karadzic said to me - I think you were there too - that Karadzic said that he offered everything to the Croats, that every Croatian village could join the Serbian republic, with full autonomy and the right to secede at a later stage if they didn't want to live with the Muslims." At page 10: "Tudjman: Is it true that we have 3.000 killed in the resistance against the Serbian aggression and 5.000 against the Muslims? Granic, the foreign minister: "2500 and 5500; right? "Boban: a little less. I cannot remember the figures now, but we do have precise figures. "President: So how many did we have with the Serbs?" The interjection is: "2500." Going over to the next page: "2500. With the Muslims? (Comment: About 5.000.) "Tudjman: We can go with that figure. 2500 killed." And what's being talked about here between the Serbs and the Croats, and 5500 between the Croats and the Muslims, so more than two times the number with the Serbs, and that's what you know to be the case, isn't it? I mean, as much as you want to talk about the fighting with the Serbs, which was non-existence in most of 1993, it was the war with the Muslims that was much more serious, wasn't it, sir? More than twice as many casualties?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they had driven us out of all parts of Central Bosnia. They have taken all our places that we inhabited --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, you didn't ask --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, Your Honours, Your Honours, please ask the witness to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen to the Prosecution's question very carefully. The Prosecution is putting extremely important questions to you, and answer the question precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't ask you why, I simply said -- my question was more than twice as many casualties -- my apologies. With the Muslims was -- my apologies. That was much more serious, wasn't it, sir, more than twice as many casualties? And that can be answered, Yes, or, No. I didn't ask for an explanation. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, the Prosecution has asked you some very important questions that one should focus on, and the Prosecution has referred to expert testimony, too, and other bases. So there was no conflict between the Croats and the Serbs, according to the Prosecution. That has been stated quite clearly. And you're reminded of a question put to a Defence expert witness. The Defence witness said, No, there was nothing going on. And then in the course of questions put to you, two figures have appeared that are problematic for me, 2.500 were killed as a result of the conflict with the Serbs and 5.000 as a result of the conflict with the Muslims. So I'm trying to see things clearly here. The 2.500 men killed, which year did that concern? Was that before 1993? Because if there was no fighting then there aren't any dead or wounded. But if 2.500 men were killed, that means there was fighting. So I no longer understand anything. The figure of 2.500 referred to by President Tudjman, he, himself, referred to that figure, what exactly does that figure concern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the number of Croats killed in the fighting against the Serbs up until the 15th of June, 1993, so mid-June 1993. As for the other part, it has to do with the ABiH all-out offensive. The fact that Central Bosnia was completely cut off. The HVO forces were completely surrounded from Konjic, Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak. The Croatian enclaves was also involved, and then at one point did they have contact with the Serbs and that was at Kiseljak. There was an incessant offensive by the armija. They wanted to deal with this, so in fighting against the armija, the ABiH that kept attacking us, we suffered terrible losses because we can't defend ourselves in an enclave if we're surrounded and attacked. So that was the problem, and not the inverted thesis of the Prosecution. You understand the Muslims had left the Serbs, attacked us from April, and especially June 1993, and they inflicted terrible losses on us. So we suffered the losses as a result of the ABiH attacks in all areas where we had to defend ourselves, because we had been totally surrounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, you haven't really answered my question, but you answered part of it. You said that the figure concerns mid-June 1993, so I have understood that. But as for the 2.500 men killed, how many of them were killed as a result of the conflict between the Croats and the Serbs? Because according to the Prosecution, there was no conflict. If there's no conflict, no one's killed, no one's wounded. If we have dead and wounded, this must be the result of something. So where were these Croats killed and wounded by the Serbs, where and when? That's what the Prosecution wants to know, and you're not answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Croats, in fighting the Serbs, suffered the most significant losses at the end of 1992, at the beginning of 1993, up until the beginning of June 1993. This was the fighting with the Serbs in which Croats were killed. Five and a half thousand killed Croats in the fighting against the Muslims, well, that occurred mostly in April 1993, and especially in June, July, and August, and up until the end of 1993 or up until mid-1994, when we had to face a terrible attack launched by the ABiH. So we had two and a half thousand men who were killed in fighting against Serbs, Your Honours; whereas five and a half thousand killed in the fighting against Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I have some difficulty in following you. You are saying that there was fighting with the Serbs and men were killed. That's line 11, page 53. And I was expecting you to tell me where. But then you go back to the subject of the ABiH. If men were killed, if Croat soldiers were killed by the Serbs -- if Croats were killed by the Serbs, rather, which municipality did this take place in? Where did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, it was throughout the territory where the Croats had organised defence against the Serbs, starting with the Neretva Valley, Kupres, Bugojno, Travnik, in the area of Usora, the area of Bosanska Posavina, then a small part of Orasje, the area where our brigades were in the Tuzla area, so throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina where the HVO was facing the VRS. And there were 2.500 men who were killed in the clashes with the Serbs. Is that an insignificant number, doesn't this show that there was fighting with the VRS? Five and a half thousand men were killed in the fighting against the Muslims. Most of them were killed in April 1993. And then up until the end of the Washington Agreement, when the Croats from Central Bosnia quite simply disappeared. On a daily basis, there were 30 to 50 people killed in Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak. And in Travnik and Kakanj, well, I won't even mention the figures there. So these people were killed in five municipalities in fighting against the Muslims. Konjic, Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak are the areas concerned, the municipalities concerned, and a smaller number of people were killed in the Vares area. So five and a half thousand people were killed as a result of the fact that we were surrounded by Muslims, and we didn't break out of that encirclement until the Washington Agreement was signed. So in Konjic, in Central Bosnia, we were completely surrounded. We had to face an ABiH attack, and at that point in time it wasn't possible for us to engage in combat against the Serbs because the Muslims had also left the Serbs and focused on us. They had inflicted significant losses on us. We lost twice as many men in fighting against the Muslims as we did in fighting against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I submit that, unfortunately, you never did get your question answered. There's no question there was fighting between the Muslims and Croats. No one denies that, and no one denies the number of killed. That wasn't the point about any of this. It was the fighting with the Serbs, and we still don't know the dates and where that occurred. I would remind the courtroom that although Mr. Petkovic talks about this being some figure that he pulls out of air as being mid-June 1993, the conversation involving Mr. Tudjman, the defence minister, Boban, and others was in February 1994. Sir -- and let me also say, Your Honour, lest the Prosecution position be mis-characterised either by Mr. Petkovic or somebody else, we have never said that -- and the statement -- the quote that I put, if we can go back to paragraph -- excuse me, slide 52 in Sanction -- because I can't really improve on this, and this was my question at the time, and I want it to be clear: "No one has ever said that there weren't some isolating fighting in places." And that's the question I put to Mr. Marijan: "Any violence, of course, is too much, and there were certainly skirmishes, there were certainly artillery shells fired from time to time, but isn't it true, sir, that in 1993, in the Prozor-Mostar-Stolac region, fighting between Serbs and Croats is not a significant factor in what was happening there? "That is true."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I put it to you, sir, that nothing you've told us so far contradicts Mr. Marijan. And, in fact, sir, you knew, didn't you, that by June of 1993, you considered the Serbs to be allies, you, yourselves?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. We never considered them allies. From the month of April, we were exposed to a total aggression by the Muslim forces, and in view of such an aggression and a total encirclement, we could not fight on two fronts. We resisted in the places where we were most at risk, and that is Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I ask you to go to Exhibit P02931, and again, I apologise to the interpreters, but I can't cut Mr. Petkovic off any other way. And unless the Chamber would graciously grant me more time, I have to control the use of the time. If you could turn, please, sir, in the binder marked "Exhibits for Cross - Tables," "Serb-Croat Co-operation" is the first one in the binder. And in this particular binder, there are blue and yellow tabs on the top. And on this particular -- there is -- once again, Your Honours, there is a table, and for the courtroom --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you repeat the exhibit number, please, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I will. P02931. It is item or line number 15 in the table. It is also tabbed on the top in blue as number 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document from you, dated the 24th of June, 1993, to Mr. Siljeg and others. And on that day, you say, sir, item 3: "I forbid any support to former allies." Number 4: "Provide support to the new allies." The new allies, sir, were the Serbs, weren't they? --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims were attacking us and bringing pressure to bear --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that, sir. The allies were the Serbs, and these are your words and said that the new allies -- and those are referring to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but I cannot allow Mr. Petkovic to continue to ramble on in an unresponsive manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, the Prosecutor has asked you a very specific question. In point 4, it is indicated: "Provide support to the new allies." And he's asking you whether those allies are the Serbs. And you tell him, Yes, or, No. There's no point in wasting time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at this point in time, when the Muslims had attacked us, the Serbs were the allies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And despite that, sir, if we can go to Sanction slide 54, despite that, sir, when you came and testified in the Blaskic case at page 24129, you were asked this question: "Tell me, General, in addition to these particular orders (related to Bosnian Serb (VRS) documents" which you had denied earlier, "how many other occasions did you and members of the HVO --" it's in Sanction: "How many other occasions did you and members of the HVO co-operate in combat operations with the VRS?" Petkovic answer, under oath: "Not once. We did not co-operate once." And yet, sir, we've just seen a document in which that was what you told the Blaskic Judges, that's what you told Judge Jorda and the others under oath. And yet we've just seen a document in which you say that as of June 1993, the HVO and the VRS were allies. And that's the truth of the matter, isn't it? That's the truth now, not what you told the Blaskic Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the truth is what I said, because we were attacked, we were being persecuted, and the Serbs were helping us out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It doesn't matter who attacked who, sir. It doesn't matter who you were attacked who. You were allies with the Serbs, and you know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. Your Honours, I think -- I think there needs to be a little bit of patience exercised by the Prosecutor. Now, I understand the frustration. The problem is context, and I believe the general wants to speak of context before putting -- giving the answer. I do think, under these procedures, because we're reminded often by members of the Bench, a variety of them that we're not in the American system where, Yes, or, No, is always the answer, whereas somebody can and does give an explanation. So if -- if I may give some advice, it might be better if the general were given an opportunity to give an explanation as to the answer. If, for instance, the answer is -- the question is, Who is your allies at this point, well, without giving the context of it, I think it's very important. And I can look at any number of conflicts ongoing what areas, whether it's Iraq, whether it's Afghanistan, whether it's Israel, whether it's -- you name it. Today's enemy may be tomorrow's friend because of the situation that is happening at that particular moment, and the general is trying to answer the best that he can. Now, it's unfair, I submit -- to take a transcript from a previous case and read the answer when, in fact, the lawyer or the Prosecutor in that case may have been pursuing a different angle at the time. So I think it would be better to allow the Prosecutor to have extra time, thus allowing the accused to give context, whereas opposed to not allowing him to give context and really restricting him to, Yes, or, No. That would be my proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, if I may add something. I agree what has been said by my learned friend, it's a question of context. But in this particular case, an exhibit has been shown parallel to this one, P2931, where there is reference to one particular location. And here in this extract from General Petkovic's testimony in Blaskic, the reference to a different location, to a different region. And now the Prosecutor is generalising these things, and General Petkovic is answering. Simply, they are not -- they are talking at cross-purposes. They're not talking about the same thing. The Prosecutor is raising details to the level of a general conclusion, and we can see from the document that the reference is to a particular location, just as in the Blaskic case the reference is to a particular location.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I be allowed to add some argument regarding the fundamental difference between this document and the extract from the Blaskic testimony? In the Blaskic case, there is reference to co-operation and combat operations --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I object. This is what we do every time. Counsel gets up and is testifying and stating her case in front of the witness, and we do this all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, I really wish to say this. And if I may be allowed a re-examination, I will show you how Colleague Scott has systematically erroneously presented the context of certain statements, and this is one such example. In this document, there's reference to co-operation in military operations with the Army of Republika Srpska, which is one issue, and the document sent to a different operational zone, the North-Western Herzegovina, there is mention of specific villages and there's no mention of combat co-operation with the VRS, and there's no reason for us to confuse these two things. And if Colleague Scott is helped by mixing up things, then that is a sad business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, Mr. Scott, I would like to remind you that there was a general question in the Blaskic case between -- the co-operation between the HVO and the VRS, and it was not linked to Ahmici. The question was a very general one, as we can see on the screen. And you have answered: "Not once," that, We did not co-operate once. That is what you said. And now we have a document in which there's not the word "co-operation," but the word "support," but let's not play with words, which appears to contradict your testimony under solemn declaration. What is your comment? There's no need for counsel, because you are responsible. It is up to you to respond.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was shown a document on the activity of the Serbs from Vlasic which was not in order. The Serbs from Vlasic did not act upon the request of the HVO, and in the document it says, Use it for propaganda purposes. In this document, Travnik has fallen, so has Kakanj, and they're advancing towards Bugojno. So tell me, if the Muslims have taken Travnik, Kakanj, and are marching towards Bugojno, how can they be any allies of mine; whereas the Serbs are taking in Croats who are fleeing to the area under the control of the VRS? Then who is my ally? These are taking in Croats that are fleeing from the Muslims, and these others are attacking us. Who has mobilised the Muslims against the Croats in Kakanj and Travnik in June? And, again, these are areas in the direction of Bugojno. What could one do in such a situation? The Muslims won't stop their operations, and the Serbs take in civilians and a part of the military that is fleeing to their territory. And that is the truth that we need to talk about, and not about allies or non-allies. Allies should not have attacked me in Travnik and Kakanj, and taken over those towns, and then gone on to Bugojno, and the previous enemies are taking in civilians and a part of the military that is fleeing. And then who is an ally and who is not?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise, but now I have had a chance to look at the transcript page 24129 from the Blaskic case. And the Prosecution of this Tribunal has shown you this answer as if it consisted of two sentences; but the answer, in fact, consists of six lines, and the continuation of this answer would show you the context in which this answer was given. And I consider this to be another example that the Prosecution of this Tribunal is not authentically representing the testimony of General Petkovic in the previous cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, Mr. Petkovic, because you have confirmed, in fact, that the Serbs were your allies at exactly the time that I told you that they were. So I'm glad that we've finally come to agreement on something. Sir, your question -- the answer you gave in Blaskic to a general question, I persist, and when we have time, when we don't have a witness in the room, we can spend hours debating the transcript, and I'm happy to do so. The general -- as President Antonetti put to you, there was a general question put to you. You answered it categorically, sir, and you knew exactly what you were saying: "Not once. We did not co-operate once." And that, sir, answer was just fundamentally false. And we have before us now, in this binder, as represented in this table -- and we don't have time, unfortunately, sir. Again, I wish we did. Forty-six documents, and the number could be double or triple that, between the 10th of March, 1993 -- the 10th of March, 1993, and the 17th of January, 1994, documenting extensive co-operation, combats co-operation, between the HVO and the VRS, many of which directly involving you, sir. Line 5, Petkovic to Rajic. Line 6, Petkovic to Kiseljak HVO. Line 8, Rajic to Petkovic. Line 9, Petkovic to Rajic. Line 10, Rajic to Petkovic. Line 11, Blaskic to Petkovic. Line 12, Rajic to Petkovic, et cetera, et cetera. You told the Blaskic Judges, "Not once, we didn't co-operate once." And you lied under oath, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I know what it was referring to and I was respond to what it was referring to. When we took over ammunition, when they gave us ammunition, I accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you weren't talking about ammunition. You were talking about combat operations, artillery support. Look at line 25 in the table as one example -- sorry, my apologies. Let's start with line 21, just to get the characters, line 21, Exhibit P09963. You're talking about an agreement which was agreed between two chief commanders of the two sides, General Petkovic and General Mladic, and between Mr. Bruno Stojic and two chief political leaders from your side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Scott, the number of the document has not been recorded, and it would help us to find it if we had it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours. P09963, line 21, and it's also flagged as number 21 in the blue tabs on the top of the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to also refer you to, sir, because I don't have time to cover all these individually, but to line 25, P09965, same format. It will be marked as tab 25 in the binder: "On July -- on July 1993," and there may be a day missing, "At their invitation I contacted the XY side." You know, don't you, sir, that the XY side was a term frequently used by the HVO to refer to the Serbs, don't you? There's no translation, apparently. Hello? Are you getting translation now? Is there translation now? All right, thank you. Referring to P09965: "On July 1993, at their invitation, I contacted the XY side." Sir, you know, don't you, that "the XY side" was a term frequently used by the HVO to refer to the Serbs and the VRS; correct? We can see it in this table many, many times, and it's very clear, sir, who's being talked about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "That major-general --" item 1: "That Major-General Petkovic should meet with General Ratko Mladic at Hotel Plaza in Herceg-Bosna on 7 July 1993." Skipping to item number 4 toward the end: "At this moment, we would need from them heavy artillery, Howitzers, which should be positioned deep in the territory of the municipality of Kiseljak for artillery support of Fojnica." Line 32 in the table Exhibit P03677, Glasnovic to Siljeg: "I made contact with the third side via hotline. They agreed to help us, and they can start shooting immediately. Therefore, it is necessary that you determine the targets to be hit, and our side should do the same." Sir, if we had the time, we'd go through all 46 documents, but we don't. You know full well that the HVO and VRS during this time-period were engaged in extensive co-operation, not only trading arms and ammunition, oil, and other materials, but actively engaged in combat operations together against the Muslims, providing the -- providing the HVO with artillery support on request, et cetera; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We purchased all that from them and we paid for it, and that is the truth, and at very high prices.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You paid for what?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the ammunition, artillery, and the treatment of men. We paid for all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you gave them the grid references and said, Open fire on this ABiH target, how much did you pay the Serbs for that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, about that particular case. I know that we did order grenades and mines, and we paid for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you're doing it again, sir, and you know full well. You're trying to waste time. I put to you the question very clearly, unless there was a problem in translation: Combat operations, not buying weapons, not buying grenades, not buying rifles, not buying tanks, combat operations, including active artillery support opening fire on Muslim positions, that's what my question is, and you know it, sir. That's the truth of the matter, isn't it, that that's what happened extensively throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have happened, but not in the way you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And now, sir, you told the Blaskic Judges, under oath, that it didn't happen once, We did not co-operate once. That's what you said, sir, and that was not true, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about this document. I was shown a document from Vlasic which I denied, but this document is one I see for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, once again, the fact that you gave false testimony in the Blaskic case is somebody's else's fault, sir; is that what these Judges should understand? I don't need any comment from Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I knew, I testified truthfully. But things I hadn't seen were things I couldn't testify about in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you didn't remember these 46 documents, and if I showed you 46 more, you'd say you didn't remember those either; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every document addressed to me, I remember, but correspondence in a different zone is something I cannot be familiar with because it is not directed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, not only did you engage in artillery -- did the VRS provide you with artillery support, but in the case of action against the town of Zepce, which was being held by the ABiH at that time, and we'll come to the date in just a moment, you and the Serbs actually carried out joint combat operations to take that town, didn't you, in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Look at line 1 of the table, Exhibit P01643 --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 1993, there was nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Item 1, P01643. Lozancic to Stojic and Boban: "The political situation in the municipalities in Zepce are growing more complex. Please discuss our position urgently at the highest level. It is necessary to initiate talks with the third party as a possibility of a solution for us in Usora." Go to table line 7, Exhibit P02805: "Zepce. The Serbs are fully observing the cease-fire on all lines toward us. They are continuously fighting in parts where the Muslims are. Serbs, headed by Colonel Arsic, commander of the OG Doboj, are offering full co-operation and joint fight against the 'balijas' in these parts." Table line 24 -- line 24, the 1st of July, 1993, P10884: "At around 1300 hours yesterday, the town of Zepce fell into the hands of the Ustasha and Chetniks. Before the town fell, they called the commander of our 319th Mountain Brigade to negotiate, and he agreed." The HVO and the VRS together conquered the town of Zepce in July 1993, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Zepce was continuously under the control of the HVO. Zepce was never lost by the HVO, and it was constantly under the control of the HVO, the entire municipality of Zepce. Had it not been like that, then there would have been no Croats in Zepce at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So I want to ask you to go to the next -- to another table in the same binder. You'll find a table that is titled on top "HVO-Serb Co-operation in Vares." It's behind a green tab divider, if you will. But you'll find the table titled "HVO-Serb Co-operation in Vares," in the same binder, and again these have the yellow tabs on top. And, again, we don't have the time to go through this, but based on -- in detail, I mean. And based on what I just showed you a moment ago, I put to you, sir, another 23 documented instances between the 9th of September, 1993, and the 12th of November, just a short -- relatively short period of time, 23 instances of extensive HVO-VRS co-operation in the area around Vares and Kiseljak. And you know that to be the case, don't you, sir? A number of these entries are directly to you: Line 1, P04907 Emil Harah to Petkovic; line 13, P05898, Rajic to Stojic, and Petkovic; line 10, Rajic to Prlic, Praljak, Stojic, and Petkovic; line 12, Rajic to Stojic, Praljak, and Petkovic, et cetera, et cetera, sir. And you know full well that you and the VRS were co-operating extensively in the Vares area in the fall of 1993, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just a proposal for us to establish contact in the month of September, and then in November we were expelled from Vares onto the territory that was under the control of the VRS. We see something that somebody proposed, and we should then see what actually happened to see the difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Line 7, P09812, 24th of October, 1993, at the time of Stupni Do; 24 October 1993, a report from the Ban Jelacic Brigade to Rajic: "Support in artillery by XY carried out." Now, that's not a proposal, sir. That's a report that the artillery support by the XY side, who you know to be the Serbs, was, in fact, carried out, wasn't it? --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document from the OG, and it never reached the Main Staff, so nobody knew whether things had been done or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, are you saying that all these documents -- none of these documents on here, including the ones either from you or to you, you didn't know about, they didn't reach you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only documents sent to me and received by the Main Staff are -- could be known by me. As for the others within the OG, as their internal communication, there was no way for us to know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Rajic -- Mr. Rajic was communicating to you on a very frequent and regular basis, and he was reporting this information to you over and over again. He was your man in the Vares-Kiseljak area, wasn't he, and he was constantly arranging deals with the Serbs, buying arms and equipment, buying artillery support? Mr. Rajic was your man in Kiseljak and Vares, wasn't he, and he was keeping you informed on all these matters?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivica Rajic was in charge of the defence of the area, and he was duty-bound to put up resistance against the Muslim aggression by hook or by crook.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And he was duty-bound to keep you informed, wasn't he, sir? I know you want to talk about everything except answering my question. I know that, sir. But he was also duty-bound to keep you informed, to report to you, as one of his superior officers, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can look at all of the reports that he sent to me. I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look at P -- line 3, P05898. Mr. Dusko Kovacevic or Kovacevic, whichever it is, and my apologies, that gentleman was the RS -- the Republika Srpska minister of defence, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic reports to you on the 15th of October, 1993: "Today I met Mr. Dusko Kovacevic," and my apologies again, "briefly. Everything is in order and proceeding according to plan, but General Milivoj Petkovic has not arrived yet. Please, do what you can to speed up his arrival, because things might get worse for us if more time is allowed to pass." You were -- you knew and you were on your way to Central Bosnia and to the Kiseljak area by mid-October 1993, a short number of days before the atrocities at Stupni Do, and you knew that that action ultimately would involve the co-operation of the VRS, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no co-operation with the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you've told us that so many times before, and we've seen the contrary. And Mr. Rajic reports to you: "Everything is in order and proceeding according to plan ..." There was a plan between you, Mr. Rajic, the HVO, and the VRS about everything that was going to happen in the Kiseljak-Vares area in the next 10 days, wasn't there, including what happened in Vares and Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has nothing whatsoever to do with Vares.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object. Could my learned friend explain the factual basis? Otherwise, we'll be in the dark about what happened next, and the witness cannot answer. If my learned friend is saying that the action in Stupni Do was planned 10 or 15 days before and that this document refers to what happened in Stupni Do, then he should be directing -- the insinuations and suggestions by -- on the part of my learned friend are inappropriate for this trial, I should think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you go next, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, your microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you go next, sir, to table line 4 -- my apologies. Table line 2, which is Exhibit P09823, this is from Mr. Rajic's journal entry for the same day, 15th of October, 1993, meeting Kovacic: "Petkovic must urgently -- everything has been arranged. Everything is happening according to the plan. Just get in touch with Mladic. This is a big task, and it has to succeed 100 per cent. We are getting into extremely favourable situation here, and next to follow is a definite solution for the Krivaja Valley. This has to be solved immediately and before winter. Borders should be established and normal life resumed. "Petkovic will command deployment of our and their troops. These are the words of the supreme commander." And that was the plan that was being put in place, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These were Ivica Rajic's assumptions and requests. Nobody was in command of the Serbs -- Serb forces, and the least so Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you go next to table -- to the table line 19, to P06478.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, when we look at this document, Rajic says, and he mentions you in the first line, "that there is a plan," that is quite clear - we are looking at the document - "that you are going to be in command of the deployment of our troops and theirs." "And theirs." And he adds: "These are the words of the supreme commander." So he's obviously referring to Mate Boban. So unless Mr. Rajic is a fool, who is writing anything, which may be the case - we don't know, but that is what is written here, and it was written on the 15th of October. And a Judge, who reads this, asks himself, first of all, whether there was, indeed, a plan, and whether there was an agreement between the VRS and the HVO. So you are still claiming that you were not "au currant" with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, those were Rajic's attempts to defend the area of Kiseljak, and he tried to link up Petkovic and Kovacevic, if needed, in order to agree the things that had to be taken, and he continues to say the condition for the passage of the convoy is 30.000 litres of petrol. And he says that Ivica Rajic is trying to agree with the Serbs to receive the material that the HVO could send to Kiseljak, and that is the long and the short of it, nothing else. And this is also the price that we were supposed to pay if the convoy was to be organised from Herzegovina in order to avoid the charges imposed by the Serbs for such an expensive ammunition. That was that, and I was supposed to arrive and agree on the details. So this is about the convoy, the convoy with the ammunition that we should have sent from Herzegovina to avoid paying the Serbs through the nose, and we would have paid the passage of that convoy in kind; in petrol, as he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listening to you, I was looking at the B/C/S document. This didn't strike me at first, but I see that all this is written in a small notebook, written by hand, very nice handwriting. And apparently it is Mr. Rajic who kept this personal diary, who describes, day by day, everything that was going on. And I assume that this notebook was either communicated by Mr. Rajic when he negotiated a deal with the Prosecutor, or perhaps it was found in the archives, so I don't know. But this document, which appears, and I stress "appears" to have been written by Rajic in realtime, and he noted everything that was going on in this notebook, you've seen this notebook?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. It was his notebook. There was no way for me to see his notebook. He's just describing his plans, and he says what he thinks that should be done. He needed the ammunition. The ammunition provided by the Serbs is very expensive. He want to do make the Serbs allow us to bring over our own ammunition because it would have been much cheaper than for us paying them in German marks or American dollars. And here he mentions the quantity of the petrol that should have been paid for a convoy that would have been sent from Herzegovina and that would have arrived in Kiseljak, carrying the ammunition that he needed in order to defend Kiseljak from the attacks by the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. The document bears different dates, and certain pages do not contain any dates at all. Maybe Mr. Scott could explain the nature of this document. Have the pages been chosen randomly, or what kind of document this is. As you can see, a reference is made to a meeting on the 15th of October. There is no date on the right-hand-side page. And then the following page refers to December 1993, and so on and so forth. It is very difficult for me to get the bearings in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have information about Mr. Rajic's notebook, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To get the details, Your Honour, and to be accurate, I'd have to double-check that. But to answer the more immediate question that Ms. Alaburic just raised, it's a matter of translation, Your Honour. If you go back to the previous page in the B/C/S version, you will see clearly the date, "15/10/1993." It should be on the screen now. So there's no mystery about that. If we could turn next, please, to item number 19 in the same table, which is P06478, P06478, line 19 of the table. This is a special report from the Security Administration of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I simply want to direct your attention to the second full paragraph of the document on page 2 of the English version: "There is reliable information that this action," and referring to Stupni Do, "above," the Stupni Do massacre, "there is reliable information that this action was under preparation as of the 16th of October this year and that it was supposed to include villages of Mijakovici, Dragovici, and Stupni Do. Information which was collected from captured members of the BH Army by the HVO leaders," making a reference to Rajic, "made the HVO units staff to reduce this action only to Stupni Do."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in fact, sir, you do know -- and as this document confirms and you do know that, as indicated in several documents we've now looked at, the action involving Stupni Do was planned around the 15th of September -- excuse me, the 15th and 16th of October, 1993, wasn't it ?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not correct. The villages of Kopljari, Ljesovina, and other features and facilities in the direction of Stupni Do were being attacked on the 15th and the 16th, so this is upside-down. Kopljari is a Croatian village, and so were the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Nothing you've said, sir, is to the contrary of this having been planned on those days. You know, you just go on and start talking, and you don't answer the question. Nothing you said is contrary to the fact that I put to you -- what I put to you, and that is the action of Stupni Do was planned on the 15th and 16th of October, 1993, regardless of what was taking place somewhere else; isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I want to object at this point. Look at the question, look at the answer. General Petkovic answered the question and then gave an explanation. Then look at the following question, and if I were in another courtroom in my jurisdiction, I would argue that -- I would object as being argumentative, this is, and also it misstates the answer. So on two grounds. So if you look at the following question, it is simply unfair, and I think that at some point the Bench has an obligation to at least point out to the Prosecutor that he can be as vigorous as he wishes, but he needs to be fair to the witness. I invite you to look at the series, question, answer, question. It is simply not fair, and I shouldn't have to be objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I believe that all the questions you have put were intended to have General Petkovic admit that the operation was prepared as of the 15th of October. That is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Petkovic, regardless of all these procedural issues, the Prosecutor is telling you that the operation was planned as of the 15th of October. What is your comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not true. On the 15th of October and around that date, the BiH Army launched an attack against Vares. It took the Croatian village of Kopljari, the Ljesnica feature, and some other features around Vares, and that's what happened. Therefore, the BiH Army launched an attack on Vares, took those features, and that, in turn, created a situation in Vares after which the commander turned to his superior for assistance because he didn't know how to control the situation from then on. There's no dispute that the HVO had lost some of its positions and that this position was less favourable from then on. There was no mention of Stupni Do, so that had nothing whatsoever to do with Stupni Do. We saw, in the case of Rajic, what happened with the Croatian village of Kopljari and other features in the direction of Vares. Croatian villages were falling, Croatian positions were falling, and Vares is under threat. Nobody mentioned Stupni Do until the moment Rajic actually went to Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're about to get into Vares and Stupni Do in a more significant way, and I know it is a few minutes early, but now might be the best time to take the break. But, of course, I'll proceed however the Chamber guides me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you wish, let us now have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the Stojic Defence has something to say or ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, thank you so much. In fact, I'd asked for five minutes at the end of the day, but it's a very short matter. We are responding tomorrow to request certification or, in the alternative, leave to appeal against Your Honour's decision dated the 15th of February, 2010, which related to the Praljak motion. Your Honour, the word limit for this is ordinarily 3.000 words. As we are combining both an application for reconsideration and, in the alternative, a request for a certification to appeal, we would humbly ask the Trial Chamber to grant a dispensation and file a document of not more than 3.500 words. We will endeavour to make it as pithy and short as possible, but at the moment, because of some authorities that need to be included, and instead of filing two separate documents, we deem it more efficient to file one document that Your Honours can consider, and that's the basis of the application. Your Honour, I thought it simpler, given the proximity of the dead-line tomorrow, to raise this in court. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, to understand well, your request is linked to the request of the Praljak Defence, that is, for a certification to appeal following a decision by the Chamber rendered in connection with 92 bis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, in relation to the documents -- the order of the 15th of February, 2010, for the admission of elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, my learned friend tells me, not 92 bis. It was the documents that were the subject of the decision of the 15th of December -- 15th of February, 2010. I think there was one order of the Trial Chamber on that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, yes. I shall consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After having heard the explanations by Mr. Khan, representing the interests of Mr. Stojic, agrees that his submissions consist of 3.500 words instead of 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, continuing on further into the topic of Vares and Stupni Do, I'd like to assist the Judges, if we can, to talk a moment about your relationship with Mr. Rajic. You and Mr. Rajic had extensive dealings with each other in 1993, and I think you told us the other day, if my memory serves, that you had probably travelled to Kiseljak in 1993 at least -- and perhaps at least, as I heard you and understood, maybe substantially more, but at least 20 times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, during this time-period, it would be fair to say, wouldn't it, that between you and Mr. Rajic, there was not only a superior-subordinate relationship, but the two of you were actually friendly, on good terms, you socialised together when you were in Kiseljak? You had a friendly relationship with each other for a substantial period of time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on friendly terms with everybody, including Rajic. Friendly in the order, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, by the time that we get to October 1993, Mr. Rajic had really had a bit of a checkered career with the HVO, he'd been in trouble and removed on previous occasions, and in fact, sir, you were something of Mr. Rajic's protector, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You protected Mr. Rajic. You intervened on his behalf on a number of occasions, and probably kept him in better standing with the HVO than he would have had it not been for you; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not true. Rajic enjoyed the same status as everybody else, and he didn't enjoy my protection if he didn't do things properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I want to -- I want to put the Prosecution case to you very clearly, sir. I put it to you that you and Mr. Rajic were close friends, you socialised frequently when you were in Kiseljak, you were close to Mr. Rajic. You co-operated extensively with him, among other things, in your dealings with the Serbs, and that you protected Mr. Rajic on a number of occasions, and that's the nature of your relations going into Stupni Do, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, sir, that you did not become aware of the HVO attack on Stupni Do on the 23rd of October, 1993? You did not learn of it on the day of the 23rd; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't learn then. I learned late in the evening after the meeting with the Main Staff of the HVO and my conversation with Zarko Tole, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's look at Exhibit P06032.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we're now changing to another set of binders. I apologise for the volume of materials, but we're now changing to what is called binder 2, but actually, in fairness, there are two parts of binder 2. There's binder 2, number 1, which includes the exhibits which were marked on the back of the binder, on the spine of the binder, P00150 to P02142, and binder number 2 of the set includes Exhibits P02182 to 5D04271. So we're going now to P06026, which is in binder 2 of the set. While everyone is orienting themselves to that, it's a document that we've seen many times in the courtroom, so I think we can go forward, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is the report from Mr. Rajic to Dario Kordic, Milivoj Petkovic, Tihomir Blaskic, and Mr. Mario Bradara on the 23rd of October, 1993. And you're saying to us again, sir, that you claim not to have received this on the 23rd of October, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it was sent to me in Mostar, and I was not in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What you said on the 17th of February, sir, at pages -- at transcript page 49613-614, in answering a similar question: "No, Your Honours, this information couldn't have reached me because Paket radio doesn't recognise my name and surname. It only recognises the station to which it is sent, which was Mostar in this case." That was your testimony on the 17th of February, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Witness EA testified, and I'm at -- making reference to -- and I'm proceeding cautiously because it's a protected witness, but I don't think, in this respect, there will be any inadvertent disclosure, I hope. At transcript page 24729, Witness EA explained this: "From an operative point of view, whoever received this message at the Main Staff, and knows that General Petkovic is not there and the message is for him, and this person knows that General Petkovic is somewhere else, then he is duty-bound to forward this message to General Petkovic. If they acted differently, then they were doing the wrong thing." And that's an accurate statement of the process and what should have happened, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not the exact procedure. The procedure was exactly what was done. When Petkovic was absent, it was General Praljak who would be informed, and that would have been the procedure and not what your witness told you that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not what you said last week, sir. You confirmed to us last Wednesday, and I covered this with you very specifically and obviously, in part, for this purpose, you testified that the procedure was you travelled to Kiseljak and Vitez often. I asked you: "Q. Did you travel to Vitez and Kiseljak and other places? "A. Yes, I did. "Q. And when you weren't physically in Mostar, how would you be reached?" Answer, Well, the duty people would know where I was. In fact, I didn't even have to tell them an address. If they knew I was in Kiseljak, they knew where I was. Your testimony was very close to that. I'm not quoting in verbatim from memory, but I think that's a fair summary. And that's the case, sir, isn't it? You knew -- you'd been to Kiseljak many times, at least 20 times in 1993. Your headquarters staff, the duty officer would have known that. And if a fax came -- or a Paket came in for you, they would have known exactly where to send it, wouldn't they? They knew you were in Kiseljak, at the headquarters, Mr. Rajic's headquarters. And we've seen even today all these documents and communications about co-operation with the Serbs, frequent communication back and forth between Herzegovina and Mr. Rajic in Kiseljak, and your people -- your people, sir, in Mostar knew exactly how to reach you in Kiseljak, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I was at the head of the Main Staff, at this time there was a commander in Mostar, that's when the commander was there. There was no need for me to receive this. Praljak did. It's not addressed to him, but you can see his handwriting down here that shows that he received it. But he's not a part of those to whom it was addressed. There was no need for me to be sought after if the commander received the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exactly, sir. Exactly, sir. You say -- my apologies, interpreters. You say, sir, that, I didn't receive it because I wasn't in Mostar, and they wouldn't have known -- essentially, what you say is they wouldn't have known where to send it, but you know that's not true, sir. The headquarters staff knew exactly where you were, didn't they? And they didn't have to know where Mr. Praljak was, but it was forwarded to Mr. Praljak. They knew how to find him and they knew how to forward it to him, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. General Praljak was in the Main Staff, and when this arrived, and it was addressed to Petkovic in Mostar, it was forwarded to General Praljak. That was the end of the procedure, and there was no need to send it to Petkovic if it had been received by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, of course there was a need, sir, because that's who your -- that's who Rajic addressed it to. It wasn't addressed to Praljak. It was addressed to you and Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic. Of course there was a reason to make sure you got it, and you did receive it, didn't you? You want to tell this Chamber you didn't receive it, but your headquarters staff knew exactly where you were, the same place you had been so many times before, in Kiseljak, with Rajic, and just like they knew how to send it on to Mr. -- excuse me, Mr. Praljak, wherever he was, they knew exactly how to send it on to you, where you were, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. General Praljak was in his office. The document arrived. It was addressed to Petkovic, as if Petkovic were in Mostar. It was forwarded to Praljak, and it was no longer necessary for anyone to look for Petkovic once the commander had received this document. And that is why the procedure as of that moment proceeded from Praljak and not from General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit P06026 in the second binder. It should be very close by, numerically, 6026. So this, in fact, is a version of the document that obviously Mr. Praljak had received, because as you said a moment ago, Mr. Praljak scribbled some information on the bottom of the page about taking -- gaining control and dealing with the situation in Vares, without mercy towards anyone. You see that, don't you, at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you received that document, didn't you, in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. This document can't be returned in this form. There's a document that's typed, there's a new document. You've seen it here, so show me that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you received a typed version, a Paket version of that document, and we've seen it in the courtroom before, and you received that in Kiseljak, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only what it says at the bottom: "Petkovic, deal with the situation," sent to the following addresses, but I didn't receive the other text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: P06028, the same binder, P06028, a Paket version of the document from Mr. Praljak, addressed to you and others, Mr. Rajic, Mr. Kordic, Mr. Blaskic. And you received that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I received this, but not the part that is handwritten at the top. So that's why I'm trying to tell you what I actually received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You received this on the 23rd of October, 1993, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So what you want this Chamber to believe is, even though the previous Paket communication was directed to you, even though your headquarters staff clearly knew exactly where you were, you didn't receive the first report from Mr. Rajic, but on the very same day, a short time later, you received -- you did, in fact, receive this Paket from Herzegovina to you in Kiseljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There was no need for it to be sent to me if the commander was there and he received it. The commander then reacted to the document. The document arrived around midnight in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You keep saying there was no need, but when someone addresses a document to a person, I put to you, there is a need for it to be delivered to that person. Mr. Rajic says, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Kordic, Mr. Blaskic. And under the military chain of command, it wasn't up to the duty officer in Mostar to decide who it should be forwarded to. I assume that what a military duty officer does is, when he receives an order, he makes sure that that document gets to the person to whom it's addressed, doesn't he, in addition to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in this case. It's taken to the most responsible person in the Main Staff, and that was the commander who received the document. If he received the document, then it's not necessary to send it to lower-ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Vinko Lucic is a person you worked with closely in Kiseljak when you were there on these various occasions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a liaison officer with UNPROFOR -- for UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, in addition to Mr. Rajic, himself, Mr. Lucic was, once again, your man in Kiseljak, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't my men. They were part of the HVO. My men, well, that just refers to my family. These were people who are part of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, these were men -- both Rajic and Lucic were men that you interacted with frequently either you were in Kiseljak or in your communications with Kiseljak. I don't know what term you would use in your language, perhaps. They were your right-hand men, they were your lieutenants, they were your preferred people for doing business with in Kiseljak, weren't they, Mr. Rajic and Mr. Lucic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't my favourite men. Lucic had to communicate with UNPROFOR and relay everything that UNPROFOR had for me or that I had for UNPROFOR. Rajic was the commander who was responsible in that area, and it was natural that if I went to Kiseljak or Sarajevo, when I arrived there, I would be with those people until I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, Lucic was a responsible officer, in your experience, reliable? Did he ever let you down?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lucic communicated in an appropriate manner with UNPROFOR. That was his main task, and he was constantly in contact with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I repeat my question: He was a responsible officer, in your experience, reliable? Did he ever let you down?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he carried out all the tasks that he had to carry out, then he didn't let me down. Why should he let me down if he carried out the tasks?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did he ever let you -- you said "if," sir, my question is a factual one. Based on your experience, the 20-plus times you were in Kiseljak, all your interactions with Mr. Lucic, which were considerable, did he ever let you down or did you find him to be a reliable officer? It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a reliable officer. He performed his tasks well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti asked you this on the 17th of February, because by the time we get to October, Ahmici has already happened. You know, sir, that was a terrible experience for many reasons for the HVO. It's a worldwide scandal reported in the international press. One of the reasons, in fact, for the creation of this Tribunal. And when you saw Stupni Do happening, you thought, This is going to be Ahmici all over again, didn't you? --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was "deja vu," some might say, all over again, wasn't it, sir? It was going to be just like Ahmici. We're going to have the internationals all over us, the international media is going to be saying what terrible things the HVO was doing, another atrocity. You knew that this was going to be -- you were afraid that this was going to be Ahmici all over again, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I have been afraid of that? I had contact with UNPROFOR, and I allowed UNPROFOR to enter Stupni Do and take the steps that they thought were the most appropriate ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to that, sir, about access and what you did or didn't do. What you really did, sir, is that you immediately, even on the 23rd, as soon as you heard this information, which I put it to you you did know on the 23rd, you immediately began what we might call damage control, didn't you? Maybe if I act fast enough, maybe if I talk to the right people, maybe if we do the right things, we can put a lid on it now. It won't be like Ahmici. We can put a lid on it and keep this from blowing up. That's what you thought, and that's what you tried to do, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not true, it's not true. The international forces entered that area. They closed the area off, and then no one could prevent them doing what they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, UNPROFOR was not able to enter into Stupni Do for some time, and, in fact, at one point General Tole issued an order to surround the UNPROFOR vehicles with anti-armour weapons and prevent them from moving, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that, and I reacted to prevent that. You have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You testified that by the 7th of November, you requested information from the internationals, but isn't it true, sir, that on the 24th of October, the very day after the attack, UNPROFOR was already asking your office in Kiseljak what had happened? It wasn't you looking for information from UNPROFOR. It was UNPROFOR looking for information from you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 25th of October, General Ramsay, who was a brigadier at the time, called me, and I spent a long time with him in discussions so that he could provide me with the information he had, if he had any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to Exhibit P06053, P06053. This is an UNPROFOR report from the 24th of October, 1993. Looking to the third page of the English version, it's under a heading, if you might be able to find it -- item numbered 9 under "Actions Taken": "NordBat II has been tasked to get to Stupni Do to carry out full reci [phoen] and search for signs of a massacre, and to check other Muslim areas and to check allegation of systematic looting by the BiH." Look at both sides: Item 10: "Informed Lucic, HVO, CO, of our concerns. Answer attached." G3: "Send letter of protest to Boban and Petkovic, seeking their intention to prevent attacks on civilians." Item 11: "As at the 24th of October at 1730 hours, NordBat II still being blocked from access to Stupni Do. Letters received from Lucic, HVO LO," liaison officer, "and Petkovic, HVO commander, which are self-explanatory, are enclosed. Verbal assurances have now been received from HVO LO," liaison officer, "of NordBat II freedom to enter all villages in the area." If we can go -- with that in mind, sir, if we can go to Exhibit 6 -- excuse me, P06049. It should be, again, close by, P06049: Let's look at the response from Mr. Lucic that is reported in the UNPROFOR document we just looked at. Mr. Lucic says, on the 24th of October, 1993: "Regarding your request for assistance in connection with the investigation of alleged massacre over Muslim population in Vares municipality, I informed it was true that a large conflict occurred," et cetera. "Any checked information --" look toward the bottom, about the middle of the page: "Any checked information about any attacking enemies of HVO Vares --" my apologies: "I do not have any checked information about any attacking activities of HVO Vares, so I doubt about the information from the Muslim side concerning the massacre in Stupni Do village. "In the annex, I deliver you an order issued by General Petkovic regarding the situation in Vares municipality. General Petkovic is personally interested for the performance of the investigation of ethnic cleansing of the villages in Vares municipality. "You have our full support." Now, Mr. Lucic sent this communication to UNPROFOR on the 24th of October, at your direction, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not according to my instructions, but he spoke then about it, and it was as a result of the fact that they didn't have the information, so he then wrote a letter to UNPROFOR on the 24th, and then I was asked to go and speak to General Ramsay on the 25th. So no one had the right information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were -- Mr. Lucic is not providing -- is not asking them for information. He's providing information, and he says: "I delivered you an order issued by General Petkovic regarding the situation." Mr. Lucic acted on your instructions in doing this, didn't he? How did he get the copy of the order issued by you if he wasn't acting co-operatively with you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Here the problem is we don't have reliable information. We informed UNPROFOR that we had no information. There was just hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, sir, you're not answering my question. I didn't say -- I didn't ask you one thing about whether you had reliable information or not. My question was -- please listen, sir. Please listen very carefully to the translation. My question was: Mr. Lucic prepared and sent this communication to UNPROFOR on your instructions and in co-operation with you, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, obviously he sent a message to UNPROFOR so that we could contact them and obtain reliable information. That happened on the following day, on the 25th, at a meeting between myself and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you, you already had information. You had the report from Mr. -- you had the report from Mr. Rajic, which I again assert to you that you had received, and you had Mr. Praljak's order that you admitted receiving also on the 23rd. It wasn't you that needed information, it was UNPROFOR looking for information, and you and Mr. Lucic sent this, as you just confirmed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said that we had no verified information. You can see that the text says we haven't got any verified information. I received an order from General Praljak that evening, and you can see that, it's obvious, but we had no verified information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go to P06022, P06022. And that's the attachment to Mr. Lucic's report he refers to. In the annex: "I deliver you an order issued by General Petkovic. General Petkovic, dated the 23rd of October, the day of the attack, the 23rd of October, Petkovic to the HVO Vares commander: "1. To control the situation in Vares, you have the authorisations to remove the following people from their present functions: Anto Pejcinovic, Zvonko Duznovic, Ivica Gavran. "2. Investigate the responsibility for the situation in Croatian and Muslim villages where, in accordance with our incomplete findings, ethnic cleansing of the population occurred. "3. This decision is to be implemented obediently." According to Mr. Lucic, sir, you had issued this order already on the 23rd of October, 1993, the same day as the attack; correct? And that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After receiving the information from General Praljak, the situation in Vares is to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that the witness is very faint and cannot be heard very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was very late in the night. That's when the order arrived at Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're being asked, sir, to keep your voice up a bit, if you can. The interpreters are having some difficulty hearing you. Sir, how did you -- what was the source of your information that it was Pejcinovic, Duznovic and Gavran who should be removed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
