utterances.text: I received the information from the commander. The situation was to be dealt with. They were to be shown no mercy. The information arrived from Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're telling us that, on the one hand, you're not receiving communications, but, on the other hand, the communications are getting all the way to Mr. Praljak in Herzegovina and back to you, that you're getting information from Mr. Blaskic in Vitez, that's somehow getting to Vitez and back to you. You were sitting in Kiseljak, sir, with an operable Paket machine and other communication, I put to you. It's simply illogical, sir, that you were not receiving these communications addressed to you. Again, I go back to what I said 20 minutes ago: Your headquarters staff knew where you were, they knew how to reach you, and you were getting all these communications, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that message wasn't returned to me. I received an order to deal with the situation in Vares and to bring in the people who were responsible. We found out --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. My apologies to the interpreters, but we have to move on. Sir, you've told -- you received the issue -- the order from Praljak, you know, Show no mercy, get things in control. Mr. Praljak's order doesn't mention any individuals by name. He just says, Go and gain control. No individuals, no names, no one identified. The next thing we know is we have a document from you, dated the same day as the attack, 23 of October, identifying these three men. Now, you say you received that information from Mr. Blaskic; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that Blaskic had information, and the Main Staff also had information. And previously I said - you've forgotten that - that information about the matter arrived from Zarko Tole, information about the people concerned. So when we checked the order, who it concerned, which people were concerned, well, that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tole, again, was another person who knew how to reach you in Kiseljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Tole was in the Main Staff. He knew where I was, and he knew how to use the phone to call me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course he did, just like your duty officer at the Main Staff knew how to reach you as well?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, but it wasn't necessary for him to return a document to me. Someone else had it, someone else who was more senior than myself was to receive it, and he received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you sent these communications -- you and Mr. Lucic sent the two documents that are marked as P06049, Mr. Lucic's letter or communication, and your order, which is P06022. You fired those off to UNPROFOR for the exact reasons that I put to you 15 or 20 minutes ago, and that is: If we act quickly, if we get some information out to UNPROFOR, if we tell them we're already taking actions, we can keep this -- we can maybe keep a lid on this situation, and then we won't have another Ahmici on our hands. That's what you were thinking, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true, that's not true. Have a look at item 2. We didn't know what had happened in Ahmici. We just assumed. Why wouldn't we have written down what you can find in that report under item 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you knew Ahmici was a crime and if we have time --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we have time, we'll get -- you knew Ahmici was a crime. You've said that before. You know it was a crime. The HVO committed it. It was the military police. And you've conceded all that, so there's no question about Ahmici being a crime. But you knew that it created huge problems for the HVO. This happens in April 1993, and now you find yourself sitting in Kiseljak, getting these reports of another atrocity in Stupni Do, and you think -- you're thinking, This is going to be Ahmici all over again. That's what you were thinking, and you were trying to put a lid on it, some people might say; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, we did not wish to conceal it from anyone. We didn't wish to conceal it from anyone, nor did we conceal it, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Despite the fact that Mr. Rajic and Mr. Tole kept UNPROFOR out of Stupni Do for some time; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when UNPROFOR made the request. But when Mr. Ramsay explained the situation to me, UNPROFOR entered Stupni Do the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: P06104, P06104, a communication from the head of the Main Staff. Perhaps Mr. Praljak: "We have received a confirmation of the Croatian TV saying they have footage of the massacre in Stupni Do, which they had received through exchange with foreign agencies." On the 25th of October, 1993, you were losing control, weren't you, sir? Events were spinning out of your control. Now the television station has footage of the massacre; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know whether the TV station had footage on the massacre. I don't know which TV team entered Stupni Do on the 25th with UNPROFOR. This is just guess-work that HTV had footage, and HTV was not in Stupni Do, and I don't know whether they had any footage from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, it's not guess-work. It's not guess-work, sir. Mr. Praljak or someone, the head of the Main Staff, said, We have received confirmation that they have footage. It's no guess-work at all, sir, so you're just flat wrong on that. Now, if you go to Exhibit P09968, P0 -- excuse me, P0 - I may have said too many zeros, P09968, this is a further document from you, sir, on the 7th of November, 1993, to Operative Group 2, Kiseljak. That was Mr. Rajic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, by now we're the 7th of November, and Stupni Do happens at least on the first day, the 23rd of October, and now it's the 7th of November. And let me direct your attention to item number 7: "UN is to be given freedom of movement, but you should record their every move. Do not allow them to move outside of the road." When you say "freedom of movement," sir, that you gave them freedom of movement some days later, that's your idea of freedom of movement, keep them on the road; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR has roads along which they go. UNPROFOR may not approach HVO positions outside the road in the area of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go back to your meeting at UNPROFOR on the 25th of October, P06144, P06144. This is when you and Mr. Lucic, and also Mr. Bandic, the Mr. Bandic that we've heard so much about, went to meet with UNPROFOR with Mr. Ramsay on the 25th of October. Item number 2: "General Petkovic knew about the possible massacre of civilians at Stupni Do." "He stressed that two HVO officers had been arrested and others suspended." He was clearly embarrassed, according to them: "HVO will investigate --" A couple of lines down: "HVO will investigate, and disciplinary will follow as necessary." Can you tell us, sir, the two HVO officers that you said had been arrested as of the 25th of October, who were they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just add that you left out that I got the information from Radio Sarajevo, which is very important. And the two officers were Duznovic and Gavran.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where did you get that information? Who told you that they had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the order said that they should be arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What order?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order dated the 23rd. Duznovic and this other man - what's his name? Gavran are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Duznovic and Mr. Gavran were not members of the HVO military. They were essentially part of the HVO political government in Vares, and they had nothing to do with Stupni Do, did they? Neither of those men stepped foot in Stupni Do on the 23rd or 24th of November, 1993, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not members of the government. Pejcinovic was. They were in the military -- Duznovic was in the military, and the other one was in the MUP, the police. So one of them was in the SIS, I think Duznovic, and the other one, Gavran, was in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Neither of those men had anything to do with Stupni Do. They weren't in Stupni Do, they didn't carry out any of the execution, they didn't burn any of the houses down. You know full well those men had nothing to do with Stupni Do. You know it now, and you knew it on the 25th of October, 1993, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information about them was such that they were the people who needed to be temporarily detained at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who was suspended -- and then it goes on to say "And others suspended," so who were they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Commander Harak, who abandoned his place, and Mr. Bozic took over from him. He was suspended and temporarily relieved of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who else? It says "others." Besides Mr. Harah [sic], who else was suspended?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other reports, but I can't remember now. Two or three officers from the Bobovac Brigade Command. I know of Harak, and there were some others who asked to be relieved of their duties --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, your communication, what you told Ramsay on the 25th of October, again, this was just your effort to feed UNPROFOR some information, again, to create the impression that you were trying to do something about the situation, but you knew full well that Duznovic and Gavran, among others, had nothing to do with Stupni Do. But you had to tell UNPROFOR something, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information about Stupni Do from Radio Sarajevo, and that was my main motive to go to Mr. Ramsay to discuss this. And these were the people against whom we took certain measures. Why doesn't the brigade commander have nothing to do with Stupni Do? He asked to be relieved, and he was temporarily relieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was talking about Mr. Gavran and Mr. Duznovic, sir. That's one of the names I gave you just a moment ago. Who in the HVO military and governmental leadership, by the time -- by this time, by the 25th of October, by the time of your other communication to UNPROFOR on the 7th of November, the one we looked at a few minutes ago -- or about UNPROFOR to Mr. Rajic, excuse me. By that time, who had you talked to in the top echelons of the HVO military and governmental leadership?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to Mr. Praljak, I talked to Mr. Tole, and I talked to Mr. Boban, as far as I can remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it was following this meeting with Mr. Ramsay that you and Mr. Lucic and the intelligence officer and your travel companion to Central Bosnia, Mr. Bandic, went back to the offices in Kiseljak, Mr. Rajic's -- the same place where Mr. Rajic was, and left the note and the instructions for Mr. Rajic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I left a document for Rajic in connection with what was happening in Stupni Do, if that's what you meant, and another document for the Bobovac Brigade, or, rather, it is one and the same document addressed to both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you knew, didn't you, around this time that the Vares Croats felt that essentially they had been sold out, the HVO in Herceg-Bosna leadership had taken the position that, you know, Vares is never going to remain part of Herceg-Bosna, it's too far to the east, it's too attenuated, we haven't even included it on our Vance-Owen maps, it's not even a Croat province anymore, and they felt abandoned by the HVO and that this was all a measure to get these Croats to move out from Vares and move to Herzegovina; that was the ultimate plan, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. Kiseljak wasn't on the Vance-Owen map, either, and it still remained; nor was Kresevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Chamber had -- and we're not going to take the time, but the Chamber will recall -- I'm not going to mention names because it may relate to a protected witness, but a communication, P05068, which sets out the position of the Vares Croats, and I take -- and I again put to you, sir, that you knew that the Vares Croats felt that events had been manipulated, that they had been sold out, and this was all orchestrated by the HVO. You knew that was being said at the time or soon thereafter, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true. Whoever lost any territory would shout that they had been sold out. This was general -- this was a general attitude among Croats and Muslims. Vares was not sold out to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go next to P06533, P06533. I believe we have a slide, Sanction slide 27. P06533 is an UNPROFOR report from Mr. Andreev to Mr. Thornberry, dated the 8th of November, 1993, about Stupni Do. And in terms of what is being said, among other things, item number 4: "... the likely answer is that the Kiseljak troops, outsiders to Vares, were needed to commit the massacre at Stupni Do." Number 8: "The HVO leader ship's intention appears to have been to force the Croat population of Vares into fleeing for fear of retaliation for Stupni Do. If so, this massacre was a war crime, made more horrible by its cold-blooded political and strategic motivation." And I put it to you, sir, Mr. Andreev hit it about right, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't accept what he wrote. Those are his assessments and his games.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you knew that the HVO soldiers, the troops, the units that were going to Vares around the 23rd of October, you know that these units had been notorious bad actors in the past, hadn't they? The Maturice and the Apostoli were problem units. They had been involved in a number of incidents of misbehaviour before that, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Scott, I would like only to ask Mr. Petkovic about the following: It happened to me that I knew Mr. Andreev from the United Nations work and from New York, so when you said that, No, I do not accept what he wrote, and then you continued, "Those are his assessments and his games," end of quotation, I would like to ask you if you have anything -- a kind of opinion or concrete events which you base your position on him, as far as when you say that those are his assessments and his games, and what do you mean by "games"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Viktor Andreev was informed by me and others regarding the position of Croats in Travnik, Kakanj, Fojnica, and he never reacted in this way. But he said, as did others, that many Croats had left. So you cannot accept, when he says with respect to such events which had happened before Vares, that the Croats had left, and he didn't take any steps. We asked him to go to Catici. There was a thermal power-plant in Kakanj. There were 200-odd Croats there, and Mr. Viktor Andreev did not want to go to Catici to see what was happening to those Croats. Therefore, I have the right to conclude that Mr. Andreev has a double standard. And, after all, I did meet with that gentleman several times during talks in Sarajevo and Kiseljak when these things happened. And when a man says on one occasion that the Croats had left, and in a second -- on a second event that the Croats had been expelled, these are not small towns, these are not minor events that were happening, then I have the right to say, of this man, that he has double standards.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I need to correct the transcript. I think it is important. On page 103, line 22, the general said that Mr. Victor Andreev said that the Croats had left, and for Muslims, he always said that he had been expelled or forced out. I think the General can confirm that that is what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite so. And this is evident in all their documents. That is what they resort to. The Croats had left, and when it comes to Muslims, then they had been expelled. And it is very hard to say of such people that they are right. I had contacts with them, and I know very well what they were doing, and it wasn't correct for them to behave in that way, you see. Because for more than 100.000 Croats from Central Bosnia, to say of them that they had left, and as for Muslims somewhere else, that they had been expelled, I think that is not appropriate, even if his name is Mr. Viktor Andreev, or his right-hand man, Mr. Benabou. We had encounters with these people, and I know and we saw what they wrote in their reports and what they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just going to show you one document on this particular topic at the moment, P11213. It should be in the second -- again the second of the -- same binder we have been working in, P11213. This is a report --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it to the back, towards the back?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, they're in numerical order, so wherever you would find P11213. Yes, toward the back. This is dated the 28th of April, 1993. It's an order from you. Among other -- number 1: "Is Ivica Rajic still in the area of Kiseljak municipality?" Number 2: "Prohibit setting fire to facilities owned by Muslims and severely punish persons who do that. Submit to me immediately any information on perpetrators. "Everything should be put under control, including treatment of civilians. In case setting fire to facilities continues, HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall distance itself from Kiseljak. "3. Prepare and submit immediately a report regarding events in the villages of Kazagici, Gomionica and Svinjarevo." Sir, you knew at the time that in April of 1993 in the Kiseljak villages, there had been a number of HVO war crimes committed against Muslims by the HVO units in the Kiseljak area, didn't you? --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true that in the area of Kiseljak some of these villages belonged, I think, to Busovaca and another group to Kiseljak, and I'm asking for information whether this is true; that is, the information I received at a meeting with Mr. Halilovic and Thebault on the 24th in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you knew -- if you didn't know on the 28th of April, you knew very soon that there were a number of HVO crimes that had been committed in these villages, if you suggest in Busovaca and Kiseljak municipalities; and you know, from your testimony in the Kordic and Blaskic cases, that some of these crimes are the very crimes that were established in those cases, that Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic were convicted of HVO crimes in these areas at these times, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were accused of these crimes. But at this time I'm trying to check whether the information is correct or not or, rather, what is going on in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And by the time you reach October 1993, sir, you had repeated information that these -- some of these units, the Maturice, the Apostoli, had repeatedly engaged in misconduct, if not war crimes, and yet it was exactly those troops and those units that you sent in to Stupni Do, didn't you? --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right; and you're not connecting to the dates when Maturice was formed. You spoke to your Witness EA, and he explained when Maturice was formed. At this time, there was no Maturice, and it was the battalion --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I know when it was formed, and existed before October 1993 because it was the Maturice that went into Stupni Do. I know when they were formed. And you know full well that by October 1993, before you sent these units into Stupni Do and Vares, you knew that both these units, among others, were highly problematic, they'd engaged in anti-Muslim conduct throughout this period, some of them were driving around Kiseljak with cut-off Muslim heads on their cars, and you knew all that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. Objection to the assertion contained in this question, and that is that the general has sent any kind of units to Stupni Do. My objection is based on the testimony of witnesses of the Prosecution, who clearly said when and who had made the decision for the attack on Stupni Do. So I appeal to my learned friend to abide by the testimony of his own witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, answer the question of the Prosecutor, and then we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not a single report on the behaviour of Maturice in the sense the Prosecutor is saying do not exist. The Maturice was formed in May, and the letter by Witness EA speaks about extraordinary people, individuals who acted correctly, and nowhere is there any report that in Kiseljak and Kresevo they had committed anything. So there is no information about Maturice which were praised by Witness EA as exemplary fighters, and there's no mention of anything bad that they had done. As for this document, the Command of the 4th Battalion was replaced, that is the so-called Fojnica Battalion and Mr. Tuka. And this was the time when, after this, Ivica Rajic took up his duties in Kiseljak. On the 28th of April, Ivica Rajic had still not taken over in Kiseljak. It was then that he came from Tomislavgrad to Kiseljak, and that is why I'm asking whether he's there, whether he has returned from Tomislavgrad to Kiseljak. As for Maturice, there is no information that the Prosecutor is referring to -- of the kind the Prosecutor is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is two minutes past 7.00. We have exceeded our time by almost three minutes. The Prosecutor will have exactly two hours to complete his cross-examination. As you know, we will be meeting in the morning, so we'll meet again at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Thank you.
